That this House protest the fact that residents of northern Saskatchewan are denied employment, and in particular the unemployed Indians and Metis, by reason of the action being taken by Eldorado Nuclear Limited in Uranium City, by importing 70 Europeans to fill current vacancies in the mine at Uranium City, there being 126 residents located within that immediate area, most of whom have been on the employment waiting list for over a year.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before proceeding with the question period, hon. members, I hope, will bear with me while I report to them the rather tragic news of the death last night in an Ottawa hospital of Gordon Dubroy. As I had indicated earlier, there was every intention, following Mr. Dubroy's retirement last spring, to honour him at the opening of parliament on October 14. He had accepted our invitation to come here and to receive what we know would have been glowing tributes paid to him by all parties in the House.
I intend to speak personally, in attempting on your behalf to somehow describe the affection and respect in which this former servant of the House of Commons was held, by saying that when I was first elected to this very honoured position, I made a personal request that he postpone his retirement in order that my first year in this office be supported by his expertise, his advice and counsel. He was good enough to do that, I think, for two reasons: first of all, because of his interest in seeing as good a performance from any Speaker as possible, and he knew that his advice would be of some assistance; and second, I think, because although he was eligible at the time for retirement, he wanted to continue to play the active and important role that he had played in advising all of us on procedures of the House. Therefore, he stayed on, much to the betterment of the performance of the incumbent in this office and much to the betterment, of course, of the precedures of parliament during that time.
He had spent some 35 years in the service of the House of Commons, and I know that he will be deeply missed by all of us. I hope I have somehow adequately expressed on your behalf the regret that we feel. May I ask all hon. members to rise and observe one minute of silence as a tribute to him.
[Whereupon the House stood in silence for one minute.]

subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF ACTION TO RESTRICT GROWTH IN MONEY SUPPLY
POSSIBILITY OF ACTION TO RESTRICT GROWTH IN MONEY SUPPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. As the United States government has achieved such satisfactory results in reducing inflation by restricting the annual increase in the money supply to between 5 per cent and 7>/2 per cent, is the government considering a policy of keeping the annual rate of increase of our money supply to a comparable range of increase, at least until the rate of inflation has been reduced to a satisfactory level?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF ACTION TO RESTRICT GROWTH IN MONEY SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are really two separate questions here. The first is restricting the rate of increase in the money supply and, second, setting out in advance the specific rate to which the increase will be kept. With regard to the first part, as indicated in the announcement of the Governor of the Bank of Canada in September, there will be an effort to restrict the rate of increase in the money supply. While from month to month there may be variations in this, the long run goal over a year will be to have a very much less substantial increase. I am advised, for example, that the effects in the payment system caused by the postal strike this month will produce an increase in the money supply. However, it is anticipated that over the year, the rate of increase will be reduced.
On the second point as to whether a specific goal will be announced in advance, this has been much discussed at length both here and in the United States. I gather there is some debate as to the soundness of the policy adopted by the federal reserve system. At the moment, the government is not advocating such a statement, although the American experience is being closely watched.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF MR. PIERRE BERNARD COUSTE, VICE-PRESIDENT OF EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
With the consent of members of the House, I should like to call their attention to the presence in our gallery of a very distinguished delegation from the European Parliament, headed by their leader, the Hon. Pierre Bernard Couste, Deputy Speaker of the European Parliament.

In calling attention to the presence of this very distinguished delegation in the gallery, I want to indicate that this is the first occasion since our pronounced intention to strengthen our bonds with the European Parliament that we have been honoured by a national delegation from the European Parliament. They will be here for several days. We will make every effort to make them feel as welcome among us as they made our delegates feel on their side of the ocean. We will certainly do everything possible to foster the spirit of friendship and co-operation between our two parliaments.

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES APPLIED FOR THE PROCUREMENT OF ANTIQUES AND CANADIANA
speechtext:
1.	What guidelines are applied in the procurement of antiques and Canadiana by Heritage Canada, the National Museum of Man or any other government agency or department for public viewing?
2.	At what level are decisions made as to the choice of such purchases?
3.	Are export permits required to sell antiques and Canadiana beyond Canadian borders and, if so (a) on what basis (b) on how many occasions have such restrictions been imposed?
4.	Does the government compete with bids received by dealers and/or individuals, for instance, from the United States, for antiques and Canadiana?
5.	Is there a maximum amount allowed for the purchase of any single item by the government when attempting to retain these in Canada and, if so, what is such amount?
6.	Does the government automatically purchase such items when their export is prevented and, if not, what incentives are there for vendors to retain antiques or Canadiana rather than sell to the higher foreign bidder?
7.	(a) What protection does the antique dealer or individual have if he is denied the right to export to a prospective purchaser outside Canada (b) is the right to export denied only because the government will purchase the item or items in question?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: that Bill C-69, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the minister going to stand up before I do?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) will really be very angry if I get my licks in first. I am sure he will have some constructive and other types of measures to suggest.
The bill before us which is designed to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act is one that deserves very serious consideration. The basic act provides short-term income support to unemployed workers while facilitating their quick re-employment. In this way, and in addition to that very important need of personal and individual help, the program assists in the proper functioning of the labour market, the stabilization of the economy, particularly in times like these, and the redistribution of income where it is needed.
Since the labour market is constantly subject to change and adjustment, as the needs of the economy and the composition of the working population alter, the act will be subject to adjustment in order to respond smoothly and effectively to those changes. I think that is doubly important when one considers the great significance of the amount of the transfer funds committed to this program, of which we are all aware.
I have mentioned on a number of occasions that the Unemployment Insurance Commission is conducting a comprehensive review of this legislation and its administration to ensure that the policy remains responsive to our needs. In July, of course, the government introduced the bill before us, Bill C-69, based on the first results of that comprehensive review. Bill C-69 is intended to complement measures outlined in the June 23 budget and is in accordance with our efforts to provide a more rational allocation of government resources. It has been developed to reflect the spirit of the 1971 act and to contribute to the achievement of one of the fundamental objectives of the ongoing social security review which is to rationalize the various schemes of income maintenance in this country. At the same time, the amendments are directed toward improving the influence of the act on the relationship
Unemployment Insurance Act
between supply and demand of workers and, in addition, to deal with some of the inequities and complexities in the act.
I should like to emphasize that the changes contained in this bill which is being presented to parliament are the results of the first findings of our review of the legislation. However, as is proper with a program of such significance, this comprehensive examination is continuing, particularly in relationship to two parallel policy developments. I mentioned one, the over-all harmonization of all our social security programs. The other is the evolution of an integrated and more comprehensive manpower policy.
We may determine that further changes will become necessary, which we will present to this House. For the present, in this bill we propose the following amendments. First, to double the maximum period of disqualification from benefits for claimants who leave their employment voluntarily, without good cause, and for those who refuse suitable employment or who are dismissed for misconduct. Under the existing act, as hon. members will recall, there is a maximum three-week period, which now will be increased in the measures contained in Bill C-69 to a maximum of six weeks. This means that, added to the mandatory two-week waiting period for all claimants, this could result in a maximum period of eight weeks in which no benefits are paid to disqualified claimants.
This amendment is being made because the number of disqualifications based on voluntary quits has been running at an alarmingly high average of approximately 250,000, plus, per year. Job refusals accounted for what could amount to an annual rate of 26,000 for the first six months of 1975. These trends have been developing in spite of high unemployment and a low ratio-a descending ratio-of job vacancies to the number of unemployed workers. To us, these facts indicate that the present period of disqualification has not been effective and needs to be increased.
We realize, and the commission recognizes, that people very definitely have the right to improve their situation and a right to secure better jobs. We do not intend to penalize those who presently want, and are seeking, work. Claimants who are disqualified under this section will continue to have the right to present their case to their insurance agent within the commission to show that they left their job for good cause. Decisions of the commission on this basis will continue to be based on long established-about 30 years-jurisprudence, so that they are not made simply at the whim of the commission officials or employers; and, of course, all these decisions will continue to be subject to appeal.
If a claimant shows that under the terms of the legislation and the jurisprudence long established in connection with it, he has good cause for his action, he will not be penalized. However, we intend to make certain that Canadians who are working hard to maintain self-sufficiency, to maintain the momentum of this country's economy, and who are contributing to the unemployment insurance program, do not have to carry the added burden of supporting able-bodied people who do not want to work.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

Unemployment Insurance Act

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Another amendment eliminates the special benefit rate of 75 per cent of insurable earnings for claimants with dependants. That rate is paid to claimants in the extended benefit period, and to those earning less than one-third of the maximum weekly insurable earnings, in the initial benefit period. Now, under the amendment proposed, that benefit rate is being brought into line with the standard rate of 662/3 per cent. The 1971 act acknowledged that the longer people were on claim, the greater would be their non-deferrable expenses, particularly if they had dependants. However, since 1970 a number of much more appropriate measures have been taken to increase support for people with families.
Most notable of these, of course, is the family allowance, which has tripled since 1971. For example, a man with three children between the ages of one and six, who received $18 a month in family allowance support in 1971, may now expect $66.24. That allowance, too, has now been indexed to rise with the cost of living. That increase, combined with the indexing of income tax, eliminates the justification for a special benefit rate for claimants with dependants.
I feel very strongly, not in any way denying the income need relative to size of family, that the use of demo-grants-in this particular case, family allowances-is a much more appropriate way to recognize the legitimate additional need based on family size, rather than through the unemployment insurance plan under which benefits are-and, I strongly believe, should be-essentially
wage-related.
Another amendment reduces the age from its present level of 70 years to 65 years at which people will no longer be covered by the unemployment insurance plan. That reduces overlapping of the program with others which are more appropriate, and provides improved support to this age group. People of this age will no longer be required to contribute to the plan, nor will they be eligible to receive benefits. The special retirement benefit, however, will be made available to persons at the age of 65 under the current conditions, that is, if they have a major attachment to the labour force, whether or not they have stopped working.
Members of the House will note that the removal of the earnings test for those who apply for a retirement pension under the Canada Pension Plan, the indexing of old age security and taxation, and the enrichment of the guaranteed income supplement which have taken place since 1971, will all combine to provide support for persons aged 65 and over, again, in my opinion, through much more appropriate methods.
Increases in these programs have been substantial since the introduction of the act in 1971. For example, the maximum retirement pension available under the Canada Pension Plan increases from $65 to approximately $130 on July 1 of this year. Old age security increased from $80 in 1971 to about $126 in 1975. The guaranteed income supplement also increased from roughly $34 for a single person in 1971 to $88 this year. In addition, the personal income tax exemption was increased by $1,000 for persons aged 65 to 70 in 1972. Last year, that exemption was indexed to rise with increases in the cost of living. Another consideration relates to the fact that it is virtually impossible-indeed,

at times almost brutal-to apply those aspects of the act which relate to availability and active job search in an effective manner to persons in this age group. The fact is that most of them have, in effect, withdrawn from the active labour force.
I know that the argument is made on occasion that these persons, having contributed premiums most of their working lives, are entitled to draw benefits from the program at the end of their careers. However, this is a fallacious argument. Unemployment insurance is like term insurance. It was designed to protect against certain situations which result in a temporary interruption of earnings. The entitlement to this benefit is subject to that and certain other specific conditions in the act. Equity, the payment of premiums, no matter for how long, does not carry forward entitlement beyond the conditions stated in the plan.
The principle of the termination of the need to pay premiums, and entitlement to benefits at a certain age, has been established for years. The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971 set that termination date for premiums and entitlement at 70 years of age. That corresponded formerly to the age of eligibility of old age security, pensions, and so on. In all these programs, this was gradually reduced to the age of 65 which is now the age at which nearly all senior citizens enjoy state income-support programs.
Another important amendment will allow an extension of the period during which insurable earnings may be counted for benefit entitlement beyond the present 52 weeks to a maximum of 104 weeks for specified groups of claimants who find themselves out of the active labour force for periods of time due to reasons beyond their control. These groups include persons who are incapable of work because of sickness, disability or quarantine, persons receiving workmen's compensation, those claimants on approved training courses, and those who were inmates of penal institutions, all of whom can find themselves unable to get work after the period of their involuntary withdrawal from the labour force and when they are ready and able to rejoin the labour force.
It had originally been thought that the shorter eligibility requirement introduced in 1971 would obviate the need for such an extension. But experience has shown us in these last four years that a number of insured persons still have a requirement for it, and in order to ensure that these groups of people have full access to unployment insurance, this amendment is being introduced. Another feature of this amendment provides for an extension of the benefit period to 104 weeks for persons receiving workmen's compensation and for inmates of penal institutions.
The fifth important amendment to which I wish to refer is one to make the availability of sickness benefits more flexible so that we will allow major attachment claimants to draw up to 15 weeks of sickness benefits during both the initial and the re-established benefit periods-a total of 39 weeks instead of the present limitation of the first 29 weeks.
Another feature of the amendment eliminates the present element of rigidity whereby the drawing of regular benefits results in a reduction of entitlement to sickness benefits. Under the new proposal, a claimant can draw up to ten weeks of regular benefits without reducing his entitlement to sickness benefits.
October 27, 1975

A further amendment under section 28 removes the provision for advance payment of benefits to major attachment claimants. In order to provide a strong incentive for claimants to find work quickly during the early weeks of their claim and draw no subsequent benefits, an advance payment equal to three weeks of benefits was made available to major attachment claimants in the 1971 act.

speechtext: It applies to hardly anyone.

speechtext:
This was provided without reference to whether they had earnings in that period, and the active job search and availability obligations were waived for that period. We found, however that in practice in 1974, for example, 85 per cent of the recipients of the advance payments were still on claim in the sixth week, whereas only 66.2 per cent of non-recipients of advance payments remained on claim at that point. Quite clearly the original purpose of the advance payment was not being served, and in order to encourage these people to find work more quickly it was decided that the provision should be removed from the legislation.
We are introducing an amendment which will allow claimants to terminate a claim voluntarily. I think this will considerably enhance the fairness and the flexibility of the program. This change is designed to accommodate certain claimants who would find it to their advantage to terminate an existing claim and establish a new one. For example, persons may establish a claim for benefit and then return insurable employment for 20 or more weeks. Under the present act, they cannot terminate their existing claim and establish a new one, so they are ineligible for sickness and maternity benefits which are only payable in the initial phase of a claim. The amendment will allow the claimant to terminate a claim where it is in his own interests and, in the process, remove an inadvertent but practical disincentive to work.
In view of the importance this government is placing on job creation in the current budget, it is appropriate that one of the proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act-this was recommended by all sides of the House-will permit the extension of coverage to sponsors of job creation programs like the Local Initiatives Program and the Local Employment Assistance Program. I have heard from all parties that it is discriminatory; the employee on a local initiative project can obtain unemployment insurance but the sponsor cannot because of the contractual relationship that person has with the government.
Another amendment which at least one member of the official opposition will welcome relates to the issuing of social insurance numbers. It authorizes the issuance of new numbers in several specified situations; for example, where SIN cards have been lost or stolen and fraudulently used. In such cases, where a second SIN number is issued the first number will become void. I have made a commitment to one member of the opposition to let him present the first new card with regard to a rather famous case which caught some attention a year or two ago.
Unemployment Insurance Act
A number of additional amendments are proposed to reduce some of the inequities and complexities which now exist in the act. One of these changes will clarify and formalize a number of powers which are currently given to the commission, through regulations, by embodying them in the act itself. These are fundamentally important and I invite hon. members, when in committee, to consider them carefully because they concern the rights and obligations of claimants.
Another amendment will allow the commission to pay the travelling expenses of persons and their representatives to attend hearings of the umpire in cases concerning coverage under the act which are up for appeal. These umpire hearings are usually held in large centres, and this change will allow appellants from remote areas to attend without imposing undue financial hardship on them.
These amendments are complemented by administrative measures which are constantly being improved and refined to make the program more effective in terms of service, control and cost. An example is the commission's special job finding and placement drive, set up a year ago last April in co-operation with the Department of Manpower and Immigration to ensure that as many claimants as possible take advantage of all the services of Canada Manpower centres. In this way, it not only assists claimants to find jobs as quickly as possible but it ensures that those who are not meeting their obligations under the act do not receive benefits.
In the 14 or 16 months of the operation of this program, some significant results have been achieved: 429,000 claimants were exposed to the program; 33,000 claimants were placed in jobs by CMC; 46,000 claimants found jobs on their own after exposure to CMC counselling; 3,000 claimants were placed on training courses; and 144,000 claimants were disqualified or disentitled from receiving benefits following Manpower reports indicating that they were not actively seeking work or had refused to take suitable jobs when offered.
The commission also achieved a number of administrative economies last year. The unit costs of performing such functions as issuing benefit warrants, processing claims, collecting overpayments and conducting benefit control investigations were all significantly reduced in 1974 in comparison with the previous year. Efforts to continue and to improve this kind of cost-saving remain a primary administrative aim of the commission.
A major amendment has to do with the formula for financing the unemployment insurance program. This program has remained unchanged for almost four years- years which have seen a very rapid and dramatic change in Canadian society and in the structure of the labour market. We believe it is now time to face practical needs for adjusting the application of the financing methods and to bring them into line with current economic reality.
When the current Unemployment Insurance Act was proposed in the white paper of 1970, it was stated that costs of the plan over and above the self-financing component would be assumed by the government in recognition of its share of responsibility for dealing with the problems which cause unemployment. At that time, a threshold of 4 per cent unemployment was set as the level above which

October 27, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
the government would assume the additional costs for unemployment insurance benefits.
That 4 per cent threshold was related to the economic conditions in the decade preceding 1970. The basic financing principle continues to hold true. Nevertheless, under social insurance principles, normal cost under the unemployment insurance program should be financed as much as possible through contributions from employers and employees. That principle was the basis for the formula in 1971, and remains the basis now, but economic conditions have changed considerably in the past five years, not only here but in most countries of the world, and it is now time to update that benchmark for calculating the self-financing component of the plan. The new threshold will be adjusted automatically each year on the basis of a moving average of monthly unemployment rates over the preceding eight-year period.
Applying this formula in 1976, the benchmark for the year will be about 5.6 per cent, a level based on average monthly rates of unemployment in the eight years preceding June 30, 1975. The regular adjustment of the benchmark will relate only to the sharing of the costs of initial regular benefits payable. The cost of extended benefits payable to those who are unemployed for longer periods will continue to be financed entirely by the federal government from the consolidated revenue fund.
Excluding the threshold change and the premium change, if the proposed amendments are fully implemented as of January 1, 1976, we can expect a net saving of $170 million in 1976 at a 7 per cent rate of unemployment. On the basis of the same assumption-and it does vary by rate of unemployment-the net increase in employee-employer cost for 1976 would be approximately $490 million, while a net reduction in government cost on these two measures in combination would be approximately $660 million.
Obviously, in consideration of the threshold to which I refer, it will be necessary to increase the rate of premiums paid by employers and employees in 1976. The employee rate, which presently stands at $1.40 per $100 of weekly insurable earnings, can be expected to rise to a level between $1.60 and $1.70. Assuming that the ceiling for 1976 will be raised to around $200 through the operation of the statutory earnings index, then the resulting maximum weekly employee premium during 1976 could range from $3.20 to $3.40. Based on these assumptions, the premium rate for employers should increase from its current level of $1.96 per $100 of insurable earnings to a level between $2.25 and $2.40. Applying the $200 a week maximum insurable earnings which we anticipate for 1976, the maximum weekly employer premium would range from $4.50 to $4.80.
The precise employee rate and maximum weekly employee premium will, in accordance with past procedures, be announced shortly, bearing in mind the requirement that the accumulated deficit in the unemployment insurance account must be reduced or eliminated, which we anticipate will be the case next year. In 1977 and subsequent years, there could be relatively small increases or decreases in premiums, depending on the trend of the eight year moving average of unemployment rates.
I said earlier that requirements for additional changes may emerge as our review continues. For example, I have

mentioned in the past that we have been examining such important parts of the program as the benefit structure. To sum up, the unemployment insurance program continues to play a vital role in the Canadian economy in terms of the protection it gives unemployed workers. The measures which are being proposed in Bill C-69 will in no way undermine that important function. Indeed, they will contribute substantially to the over-all effectiveness of this program by eliminating some rigidities and inequities, by removing some disincentives to quickly return to work, and by cost reductions and better allocation of resources.

I hear the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) saying something. He is a member of the class of '68. Let me digress for a moment. I was glad to see that this government recognized his abilities. I hope that as Minister of National Revenue he will do a good job. We of the class of '68 do not want to be disappointed. So far, members on my side have not thought the minister's job all that important. I do not want to be mean, but they are not even asking questions of the minister. Therefore, I hope the Minister of National Revenue will mind his business and let me mind mine.
Let me bring to the attention of the House some general thoughts about unemployment insurance. We must ask some questions about its fundamental role. Is it an insurance program or an income redistribution scheme? If it is an insurance program, then surely we ought to be considering a program which is designed to protect bona fide members of the work force from the effects of unexpected unemployment. If it is an insurance program, it ought to be placed on an actuarially sound footing. If it is an income redistribution program, then of course it is just that. Any program of income redistribution may be defined as a program designed by the government to shift resources from one group or level of society to another, according to predetermined guidelines. Income redistribution, by definition, considers what is normal, not what is unexpected, and takes account of actuarial principles.
If we consider whether the program should be one of insurance or one of income redistribution, we should honestly conclude that unemployment insurance should be exactly that-unemployment insurance. To interpret unemployment insurance as social security, however noble, is to misrepresent the constitutional underpinnings of the unemployment insurance concept. Canada has a plethora of other programs specifically designed for the ends of social security. The minister mentioned some of them. They form the income maintenance and social security component of our social welfare programs.
Finally, I suggest that unemployment insurance as a means of wealth redistribution is extremely regressive because all wage earners grossing more than the maximum insurable earnings pay the same premium rate. Therefore, this concept lacks progressiveness. The suggested provisions for raising the benchmark or unemployment level above which the government will intervene, will make the situation even more regressive. The current premium scale is already highly regressive as it establishes the maximum pay-in at a relatively low income level. Accordingly, the brunt of financing the program's costs will be carried not only by the upper income groups; it will be carried also by the lower middle and middle classes. Therefore, the suggested regressive financing of this income redistribution program really runs counter to every principle which the Liberals opposite hold to be true.
The other point worth raising concerns the maximum pay-out figures. The minister mentioned a period between 52 and 104 weeks for pay-out. We shall need to examine that more closely. Allowing a person to remain on unemployment insurance for a full year because suitable employment could not be found for a full 12 months or, even worse, allowing a person to collect weekly cheques for one year while that person's feelings of dignity and

Unemployment Insurance Act
self-worth go down the drain, is totally unacceptable to me, and to my party, I suggest.
It should be our view, except in the most exceptional circumstances, that unless an unemployed person can find a job within a relatively short period-say, six months- that person does not possess the requisite skill to be employable and is, in fact, unemployable. In that case, we face what economists call a structural problem. It is far better, it seems to me, to face this fact and insist on retraining, relocation or whatever is necessary, instead of letting the person sit at home and become, in fact, a new member of the welfare state at enormous cost.
It is interesting to note that the United States, which has a population ten times the size of Canada's, spent $4 billion on unemployment insurance in 1973. On the other hand, we in Canada will spend approximately the same amount in 1975 in that area. I point out that between 1940 and 1970 we spent a total of $6 million on unemployment insurance. That is how much we spent in 30 years. On the other hand, between January, 1971, and December, 1975, our unemployment insurance costs, as predicted, will rise to some $10 billion.

But the year 1975 is the year that really grabs us. Have you noticed, Mr. Speaker, the sudden and dramatic escalation in terms of costs during while the government sat on its fanny for years without even considering amendments, without even considering whether the country could afford it? In his budget address of June 23, the then minister of finance lamented this massive increase and stated that restraint would have to be introduced. However, the point to emphasize here is that the government was not really concerned about the direction the Unemployment Insurance Act was taking. On July 28, 1970, the hon. member for Verdun, who as minister of labour was responsible for the birth of this monster, prematurely declared that unemployment in Canada has passed the turning point and would thereafter show constant improvement. In 1970, 5.9 per cent of the labour force, or 495,000 people, were unemployed. This year, unemployment is running at 7.2 per cent and is expected to exceed 8 per cent, which would result in up to 800,000 Canadians becoming potential unemployment insurance recipients.
In the Financial Post of February 26, 1972, the present Postmaster General, then minister of labour, was quoted as saying that the extra costs "don't present me or the government with any problem." I can remember his saying that. Commenting on the announcement of a $700 million Unemployment Insurance Commission deficit in 1972, the Prime Minister declared:
I don't see any scandal... What if it (the fund) needs another million, a hundred million or two hundred million? What's the magic in numbers?
I will tell him what is the magic in numbers. The Canadian people are just tired of paying through the nose. Again, on May 25, 1971, appearing before the appropriate committee of this House, the minister of labour of that day said:
There is no reason for alarm and I certainly feel no reason for alarm.
Today, though, there is a great deal of alarm, to judge from the minister's statements. He says that the act as presently drafted is riddled with disincentives and he wants them removed. We on this side, accepting our responsibilities, have continuously stressed the fact that the legislation contained far too many disincentives.
The statements I have quoted show quite clearly that if members of the government were aware of the problems involved in the Unemployment Insurance Act, they were certainly not ready to admit to them, much less to deal

with them. As indicated in the budgetary address of the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner), the situation was allowed to deteriorate and it is now being dealt with in a post facto fashion. However, although the government was not ready to grapple with problems which by then had become apparent, others were quite willing to point them out. In a press release on September 25, 1972, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) put his finger on the situation. He stated:
The situation created by the government in respect of those who are working is simply this: expenditures on unemployment insurance are said to be monstrously out of hand ... The cost to individual taxpayers will be staggering.
This year, Mr. Speaker, unemployment insurance will cost every taxpayer in Canada an average of $175 above the regular premiums. My hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition, went on to say:
By its economic policy, its legislation, and by the Prime Minister's own "non-work ethic" dissertations the government has been undeniably responsible for putting so many Canadians in both these situations-unemployment due to work disincentives, and staggering taxation.
Despite these warnings, it took the former minister of finance almost a full three years to recognize that, in his words, some features of the new system, that is to say, the post-1970 arrangements, have "undesirable effects on work incentives".
I wish, now, to deal with another area. Less than a month before the June 23 budget was brought down, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) dealing with the possibility of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, stated:
The fundamental reasons why we have not brought them (the amendments) in yet is because parallel to the development of these amendments there is a very serious consideration on the part of my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the provincial ministers of health and welfare.
He went on to say:
Increasingly it is becoming apparent that there is at some stage going to be a reconciliation and a harmonization of the interface between the unemployment insurance benefit program particularly and the ramifications of it and the rationalization of the income security system.
The minister merely touched on this particular aspect- the harmonization of the two programs and the rationalization of the income security system. As I say, this address to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration was delivered less than one month before the presentation of the budget. It is difficult to believe that in one short month the executive of the present government was able to reconcile, harmonize and rationalize the working of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the health and welfare ministers' proposed income security system. If it has been able to do so, where is the minister's orange paper?
It is even harder to believe that proposed changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act were meant to dovetail with the primary objective as stated in the orange paper, because on his own admission the Minister of Manpower and Immigration believed it would be 2'A years before the orange paper would become legislation. I think this calls for some emphasis-2V4 years. In the absence of the required dovetailing, I say this is an ad hoc, cosmetic

approach to a serious situation. I refer to the bill which the minister has introduced for second reading. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration continued:
As we get more deeply into the subject (changes in the UIC) we find that almost every action we are contemplating would have some effect (on income security).
Yet, less than a month later, changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act are proposed. This is why I have some hesitation about believing what the minister says when he asks us to believe in the justice of these amendments to the act. Since we are led to believe that any changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act will invariably affect the entire income security system, where are the parallel changes in the income security system? There is no dovetailing. In fact, it appears that as of May 27 of this year, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration had no inkling that amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act were proposed in the budget.
Speaking about Bill C-125 of the last parliament, a bill concerning unemployment insurance which died on the order paper, the minister said:
I felt the measures introduced in that bill had gone too far and were not measures I wanted to see introduced ... As I gained experience in the portfolio I did not wish to proceed with the Draconian measures which were in the bill.
Yet we now see very similar "Draconian measures" being introduced in the budget, especially those which are aimed at the so-called low income claimants and the aged. The bill before us is directed toward these groups. If the minister believes that these are the people who are ripping off the system under the present act, well and good; but he will have to show us that our senior citizens are so involved. I understand there are only about 5,000 or 10,000 who would be affected by this suggestion.
The then minister of finance in his budget address bemoaned the failure of consensus. It is no wonder consensus failed when there does not even appear to be consultation among cabinet members, let alone the provinces or members of labour, business and other interest groups.
In fact, the Canadian Labour Congress, an organization which will be greatly affected by these changes, was surprised and shocked that any such revision of the Unemployment Insurance Act would be contained in the budget. They have claimed that the budgetary revisions planned for the Unemployment Insurance Act are but "a political sleight of hand" and yet another attempt by the government to shift the blame for unemployment on to the unemployed. Indeed, in face of a budgetary deficit of almost $4 billion, the government's proposal to implement expenditures restraint can be looked upon as being at the expense of the aged and the poor and is tantamount to folly. It is a cruel trick on the Canadian people. If the minister has evidence that these are the groups causing or helping to contribute to the $4 billion deficit, we are prepared to listen.
The government has proposed-the minister has gone through them-five basic changes in the operation of unemployment insurance on the grounds that the cost to the government is becoming unwieldy and that the present act contains some features which have undesirable
October 27, 1975

effects on work incentives. There can be little argument that the cost of operating the Unemployment Insurance Act is becoming prohibitive. As I have said, total benefit payments in 1974-75 amounted to $2.3 billion, with the government picking up $700 million. However, benefit payments in 1975-76 are expected to exceed $3.75 billion, placing a total cost on the government of approximately $1.75 billion, an increase of 150 per cent over the previous year.
This total increase reflects in part the increase in unemployment. Unemployment in 1974 averaged 5.4 per cent, and has been running this year at an annual rate of 7.1 per cent-an increase of 31 per cent-and there are indications it will rise to at least 8 per cent by the end of the year. However, unemployment statistics as such do not account for all the increases in pay-outs. While unemployment rose by 31 per cent, the total cost of UIC from April, 1974, to April, 1975, rose 69 per cent. More important is the fact that the length of benefit periods for recipients increased by some 51 per cent over the same period. This factor, therefore, can be interpreted as being the result of either the mismanagement of the unemployment insurance fund or a growing trend in which people feel more secure collecting unemployment insurance benefits than in the work environment.
Because of that last supposition, we in the official opposition still call for an independent inquiry into the operation of this act. Such an inquiry should examine the efficacy of the act as now constituted, and its administration. It should envisage whether changes in the legislation are required, as well as investigate in particular the administration with a view to maintaining an adequate program of unemployment insurance while avoicffng disincentives to employment and excessive costs to contributors and taxpayers.
We feel there should be a fully independent inquiry, and not some in-housekeeping sort of thing about which the minister was speaking on the part of the Unemployment Insurance Advisory Council. We feel there should be a fully independent inquiry into the workings of the Unemployment Insurance Act in order to determine whether in fact this is an insurance scheme, a welfare scheme or a combination of both, and in order to determine whether there are abuses and, to the extent there are abuses, how to get rid of them. It should inquire into the extent of disincentives and recommend how best we can remove them. This should be a full-blown, independent inquiry, and not something the minister can play hanky-panky with whenever he feels the heat is too much. We want an independent group to look at this very serious matter.
The principle we should all adhere to is that any scheme such as the one we are dealing with now should be very difficult for one to take advantage of, but it should be very easy to administer. It should be difficult to get on the recipient roll of such a scheme, and very easy to get off. Apparently this is not the case now, as these amendments would indicate.
The government has destroyed the work ethic as a result of these disincentives. This, in turn, results primarily from a statement the Prime Minister made some time ago. He said: You do not have to work for money, because there are other amenities in life which are so meaningful. I should like to ask what they are and who is going to pay
Unemployment Insurance Act
the shot. I do not mind these theories, principles and political philosophies, but I know somebody has to work in order to pay the shot. We cannot have that sort of attitude, that one does not have to work.
Furthermore, while the government pays lip service to the issue of disincentives, it only offers one point that even remotely deals with the problem, and that is the penalty period being increased by 100 per cent, from three weeks to six weeks. This would mean a waiting period of eight weeks including the two-week waiting period. This party has suggested for some time that eligibility for unemployment insurance should be based on an extended period in the work force. We still stand by that suggestion. Such an extension would ensure that unemployment insurance was directed to those who were securely tied to the work force, and as such it would be unemployment insurance and not just another welfare program open to public abuse.
The latest figures of June, 1975, revealed, in terms of trying to determine whether we should move from eight weeks to 12 weeks or to 20 weeks, that of the total UIC caseload, 15.1 per cent only have an 8 to 12-week attachment to the work force, while 34.8 per cent have an 8 to 20-week attachment. Since all recipients with less than a 20-week exposure to the work force qualify as minor claimants, that is, a 15-week entitlement, we can conclude that by extending eligibility to 12 weeks we could save $487.4 million, or 12.2 per cent of the expected outlay for 1975; or by extending eligibility to 20 weeks we could save $1,123 billion, or 28.1 per cent of the expected outlay for 1975, based on average weekly claims of $82.77 for July,
1975.	,	.
We are not saying this is the answer, but we are saying we will have to look into the eligibility period. I think that is just what the minister is doing. He said earlier that they were looking into the benefit structure. When he said that he caught my attention and my eye. However, the fatal flaw in the analysis of the issue by the Minister of Finance rests on the fact that the problems of unemployment cost in terms of disincentives are inexplicably bound together with the government's inability to deal with the real problem of unemployment and job creation.
The minister responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission has stated that the commission has a double mandate, the first of which is-
-to ensure that workers who suffer an interruption of earning receive the temporary income support to which the Unemployment Insurance Act entitles them-
The second mandate-
-to facilitate the quick and effective reabsorption of unemployment workers into the labour force, thereby protecting the integrity of the scheme.
It is becoming very clear that the Unemployment Insurance Commission is fulfilling the first part of its mandate of providing some sort of support. This can be seen merely by looking at the massive increase in payments. However, it is failing miserably at facilitating a quick and effective reabsorption of unemployed workers into the labour force. Therefore, the problem is not only one of costs per se, but it is also one of unemployment and inefficient job creation.
We all know that the Unemployment Insurance Commission would not cost the government anything if unemployment were 4 per cent; that is, employer-employee

Unemployment Insurance Act
contributions would make it self-sufficient. It therefore becomes very clear that the mismanagement of the UIC is only a manifestation of the larger mismanagement of the economy and the government's inability to attack the task of job creation in any systematic fashion.
We have had some discussions regarding the minister's five-point reform program, and I would like to run through a few of them. The first is an increase from three to six weeks for the period of disqualification for those who have quit or have been fired from their jobs or refused suitable employment. This is something that is really difficult to criticize. As a matter of fact, I do not think we can criticize it at all, because this is what has been needed. But the government certainly has taken its time in bringing in such an amendment.
One of the amendments refers to payment of premiums and receipt of benefits terminating at age 65. The minister will have to explain this to my party. If he feels these are the people who are ripping off the fund, he will have to provide a good deal of proof. I do not like the minister talking about demogrants when it comes to unemployment insurance. Surely, if I have $1 million in the bank and receive income through working, that income would not be taken into consideration. Because I have income from $1 million and have lost my job, I would not receive unemployment insurance. That is what the minister is trying to say with regard to these demogrants. That has nothing to do with earnings and a man's entitlement to unemployment insurance.
Then we are told that the provision with respect to the special benefit rate of 75 per cent to low income claimants with dependants eligible for extended benefits will be brought into line with the standard benefit rate of 66 2/3 per cent. Once again, the minister talks about demogrants and family allowances. What has that to do with the next proposal, whereby the premium a person shall receive can be up to 75 per cent? He wants to confuse the issue and say that because the children are receiving the money, it is not necessary to give the man any money. Then there is the provision concerning the extension of the period during which a claim can be made and benefits received for those suffering temporary disabilities or special training courses. I am not too sure what that means. This section is so nebulous as to be incoherent. We know that in due time the minister will explain this.
Then we have the change in which the claiming procedure for sickness benefits will be made more flexible by allowing eligible recipients to receive such benefits at any time during the first 25 weeks on claim, rather than the first 15 weeks. This change is really no change at all. It is merely an added courtesy to those workers who fall ill, by allowing them the option to choose when they wish to receive benefits. In no way does this provide for restraint. It could result in a slight increase in expenditure.
In respect of the new government-employee adjustment procedure, as mentioned, unemployment insurance operates entirely on the basis of employee-employer contributions when unemployment is 4 per cent or less. The present minister has claimed that an unemployment scheme like ours does have a crucial role to play in keeping the economic ship afloat in an industrialized country, and that this is something we should recognize when we examine the cost of a program like this. This was referred to on May 27, 1975, when the minister appeared before the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
Given the proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act as outlined in the budget, it is apparent that the government has abdicated its belief in the worthiness of unemployment insurance for those who truly need it; that it has reneged on its commitment to fight unemployment, and that it is incapable of stimulating creative job creation programs. By changing the 4 per cent unemployment benchmark to an eight-year moving average, and by doing so during a recession, the government is ensuring that little or nothing of the additional cost of unemployment insurance which accrues from its inability to deal with unemployment will fall on the federal treasury in years ahead.

October 27, 1975

Since this reneging of the clearly established benchmark of 1971 makes it apparent that the government is no longer committed to 4 per cent unemployment, and since a great need still exists for unemployment insurance irrespective of the government's posture, it is safe to assume that the total cost of unemployment insurance will remain exorbitant and will probably even increase. The point is that now the burden for the government's ineptitude will fall directly on the shoulders of the taxpayer through what is in fact a new form of payroll taxation and, at that, regressive taxation of the worst ilk.
Don McGillivray, a financial analyst, writing for the Financial Times estimates that the change in unemployment insurance financing faces Canadian employees and employers with an additional tax burden at least twice as heavy as the extra tax on gasoline, and that this extra payroll tax under the new formula may reach $800 million to $1 billion next year. This new tax load will amount to an average of $89 or more a year from the wages and salaries of all Canadians who work for a pay cheque.
In addition, since the eight-year averaging formula will progress with time, it is safe to assume that this tax burden will increase as the formula moves, becoming more subject to the government's abysmal unemployment record. Even more alarming is the fact that this new form of taxation is highly regressive. Since premiums paid are based on a maximum insurable income of $185 per week- a level which is below the average Canadian income at present-anyone making $9,620 or more annually will be subject to the same tax. Therefore, this innovation shifts the balance of the tax system away from the income tax, which is termed progressive, to a payroll tax which bears most heavily on the poor because they are levied at flat rates and have a ceiling beyond which no additional tax is paid no matter how high the income. Mr. McGillivray stated in his article:
Sooner or later, Canadians will have to ask themselves whether they want to finance such plans from taxes which bear most heavily on those least able to pay.
There are several other minor revisions on which I would like to comment briefly with respect to the minister's major amendments. The minister said that someone on this side of the House indicated that sponsors of government programs such as LIP and LEAP will now be insurable and eligible to collect unemployment insurance benefits. I do not understand that thinking and I will have to drag it out of the minister. Here the minister and his government create unemployment, which is something we certainly do not accept, and in creating unemployment they tell people what to do and how to do it by way of short-term employment, and after that they want to pay them unemployment insurance. I do not accept that and the minister will have to explain to me in no uncertain terms why this approach is viable and necessary.
I was pleased to hear the minister state that under exceptional circumstances a member of the work force can now receive a second social insurance number, under section 34. This section makes provision to eliminate the possibility of two persons having the same number, one person having two numbers, or the fraudulent use of another person's number. Social insurance cards will also
Unemployment Insurance Act
serve as a form of national identification without which no job can be obtained or held. We welcome that. It is through the tenacity and the aggressiveness of the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan) that this amendment has been pulled from the minister's clutches, in light of the hardship suffered when someone had his social insurance card stolen.
I will conclude by stating that we on this side of the House do not believe these amendments go to the root of the problem. We certainly endorse amendments which we believe will bring insurance principles back to the Unemployment Insurance Act, but at the same time, when it comes to spending $4 billion we want to move with caution. We remember well when we wanted to move with caution with respect to the removal of the $800 million ceiling, and the government wanted to hurry the bill through the House because otherwise, they said, the unemployed would not get their cheques. We will not be fooled again in the same way and we will certainly take our time.
Many of my colleagues want to take part in the debate on this bill. They will have more to say on the various matters which I have brought to the attention of the House but-this is most important-when the bill goes to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration we want to make sure that as a result of amendments the minister will bring in an unemployment insurance act that is an insurance act per se.

Mr. Speaker, it used to be quite refreshing to listen to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) when he spoke on unemployment insurance matters, but having listened to him for three years it has become monotonous. I wonder whether the hon. member has ever gone east, where unemployment in Newfoundland is between 16 per cent and 20 per cent; to Nova Scotia where it is about 9.1 per cent; to New Brunswick where it is about 10 per cent; and to Quebec where it is 9.3 per cent to 9.5 per cent and I wonder whether he has made these great speeches about the work ethic and how the unemployment insurance pay-out is part of the great rip-off which cost the rest of the Canadian taxpayers $2 billion last year in pay-outs to benefit recipients.
I dare say they keep the hon. member on campuses at universities where he can safely make these great, statistical speeches, because I have heard other members of his party from the disadvantaged areas of the east and the north speak in favour of unemployment insurance benefits and even ask for extensions for their constituents.
We hear all these numbers thrown out, billions of dollars mentioned, statistics quoted. Let me point out, however, that the unemployed are not statistics. To be unemployed is a real and cruel experience. Remember that these people are unemployed through no fault of their own. Often their unemployment results from action by federal, provincial or municipal governments, or, in the private sector, because a corporation has changed its pattern of production in the interest of higher profits.
The hon. member for Hamilton West spoke about the work ethic. I always thought the idea was to teach our children to use their abilities to their best advantage in whatever situation they found themselves. Surely it is not above reason to expect that a person who embarks on a job

Unemployment Insurance Act
should get satisfaction and enjoyment from it as well as remuneration. Surely it is not only work for the sake of working; there must be some enjoyment that one gets out of work. On the other hand, the minister was reading from what the Unemployment Insurance Commission had typed up for him. He came here and read it in a deadpan way as if he were trying to downplay the whole issue.
My party is not prepared to have its members make one or two speeches and then let the issue die, because the issue is more important than the unemployment insurance fund; it is far more fundamental than the fact that we have to put $2 billion or $900 million, or whatever the figure may be, into the fund. Surely the question is what the government is prepared to do about unemployment. The problem for the House is not to sit down and devise the finest and most perfect unemployment insurance act, but it lies-and the government must bear full responsibility for it-in the whole question of employment.
The government must accept fully responsibility for having failed working Canadian people because we have to pay for those who are not working, as well as the unemployed who have to face unemployment with limited incomes and must wade through the bureaucracy of the Unemployment Insurance Commission which often makes them wait for weeks before they get their benefits. I know something about this because it happens in my riding. I see the commissioner up in the gallery, smiling away. It is not a smiling matter at all. Surely, if these unemployed people are entitled to benefits there ought to be no delay. Though I must say, about that gentleman, that he has been most co-operative in dealing with some of my more serious cases.
When I see the government proposing Bill C-69, it reminds me of the story of the robin. A certain robin thought, when the fall came, that he would stay up north because the weather was very mild: there was a warm spell and he thought he would not fly south, although that was what his fellow robins did. As the fall progressed, the weather became colder, until December came and it was extremely cold. At that point the robin decided he could not stick around any longer and he ought to fly south. He went up into the air and started flying south. Of course, the air was cold and his wings became frozen. As he started to fall toward the earth, his wings being iced up, he said to himself; "I know I am going to die; the end is near."
The robin fell into the barnyard of a farmer in my riding. As he lay there on the frozen ground, eking out his last breath of life, he thought that the moment had come when he would die. The along came the farmer's horse and defecated on the robin. Then robin started to feel the warmth spreading through his wings and the ice started to melt. He was feeling so good about this that he began to whistle, because that is what robins do when they are happy and warm. The farmer's cat happened to be prowling through the barnyard, and as soon as the cat heard the whistling he tracked the robin down under the mound and popped him into his mouth. There are two morals to this story which Liberals and Conservatives ought to keep in mind: not everyone who defecates on you is your enemy, and not everyone who digs you out is your friend.

speechtext:
There is a meaning there, and when we think about it both sides of the House will see the connection between that little story and what this government is offering us in Bill C-69. The history of what is proposed by the government with respect to the Employment Insurance Act began back in 1971. Hon. members will recall that that was the year the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) fought his first fight against inflation, and of course it was quite a battle. At that time he said:
I'm afraid there are a lot of people in this country who are bargaining that, oh well, this government can't hang tough (in its fight against inflation) too long because it will be frightened when it sees unemployment go up to 6 per cent... But if the people think we are going to lose our nerve because of that, they should think again; we're not.
That is what the Prime Minister said when he began the first salvos against inflation-and inflation is always fought on the backs of workers, poor workers and workers who are not organized. That battle was fought, but lo and behold, the gentleman who is now the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) came like the white knight on a charger and delivered to parliament an unemployment insurance bill in 1971. He was like the horse. We had before us unemployment insurance legislation which widened the scope of unemployment insurance coverage for that great battle with inflation. At that time, the threshold for unemployment was set at 4 per cent, and it was argued that anything beyond that 4 per cent would be picked up by the government and paid out of the general operating revenues. We know what happened: the 4 per cent unemployment figure became an unrealistic figure. We must remember that one of the arguments put forward by the then minister of manpower and immigration who was responsible for the legislation was as follows:
Our system is really on trial if we cannot operate on the basis of lower rates of unemployment that have been traditional.
As a matter of fact, he was saying that that 4 per cent threshold would indeed act as an incentive to the government so that it could go about creating employment and so that there would not be a drain on the fund and on the taxpayers of Canada if unemployment should go over 4 per cent. I must say, some incentive!
What is being proposed? Since that threshold has not been an incentive, and of course the government and the minister may not want to be trapped into any such predicament in the future, what is the government prepared to do now? It is prepared to adjust the situation based on the previous eight years of unemployment rates, and of course that figure will float upward as has been the case in the past. It never floats downward, it floats upward, and of course more and more of the cost will be picked up by those who are working. It seems to me that this is a very regressive form of taxation. Those who are working will pick up more and more of the cost of the program. The government will shift from its shoulders the responsibility for its bad planning and for the lack of programs which it ought to hring into this House with respect to employment.
October 27, 1975

What is the government going to shift in this particular amendment? It is going to shift its estimated $900 million for 1976 on to the shoulders of small businessmen and those who are working. This is a very regressive form of legislation. It is only one of three pieces of regressive legislation we have seen emanating from the June 23 budget. We saw one which imposed a 10 per cent excise tax on gasoline. That tax penalized the working poor, the handicapped and those who live great distances from their jobs. We fought that legislation, but the government had its way.
The second regressive move is the announcement that the government is limiting its contribution to increases in the cost of medicare. Again, taxpayers face an indirect form of taxation; again a regressive taxation will be foisted upon the working poor.
Then there is this particular bill, and I suppose these three items could all be summed up under what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has called "rough justice". First, the government creates unemployment, in the true Keynesian fashion, to fight inflation. Then the people start collecting unemployment insurance benefits; and now they are being blamed for their own predicament and being told that the government has to get tough with them.
We have seen how the government gets tough. The government can get tough when it deals with the little people, but when it deals with large corporations it sets up committees to study their structures but never to come to grips with the problems. It seems to me that when it comes to that kind of fighting, the government is great at doing battle with those who can least defend themselves. I find this very strange indeed. Here we have a government which just last week brought in an anti-inflation program which, according to the government, will fight to keep the lid on wages and prices. It turns out that it is only a lid on wages and not on prices at all. Prices can keep going up. In fact, the Prime Minister told one lady that prices will go up. That is small comfort for the unemployed and for those who are not organized in unions and probably earning only the minimum wage.
Even where there is an organized operation, such as that at Elliot Lake, the conditions are such that workers are forced to accept them or, I suppose, to refuse to work and be counted in that 23,907 the minister rhymed off in his blurb as "having refused employment". It seems to me that this is the situation; it is great to restrain poor people, but when we come to the rich and the powerful it is another story.
As I have said, the new proposal will change the level at which government contributions are triggered from 4 per cent to an average in the last eight years. It seems to me that in 1976, if the present unemployment rise continues, we could see a benchmark of 6 per cent in 1977. In just the same way the government argued that keeping a 4 per cent ceiling was an incentive for the government to keep unemployment down, it appears to me that putting it on a floating scale would just be opting out of their responsibilities completely. They are using it as an escape-hatch from their responsibilities, knowing they did not show any concern when they were taking it out of general revenues. Surely now, when they are proposing a system to take care
Unemployment Insurance Act
of those increases automatically, they will show even less concern.
I should like now to look at the question of who is going to pay, and why this party claims this is a regressive tax. The present maximum earnings which are insurable are approximately $8,500. Since about two-thirds of the work force is unorganized and most earn below $8,500, these are the people who are going to pay increased contributions to the unemployment insurance fund. That is why this party takes the position that this is a regressive step. The bosses get the benefits. So far, all we have heard from the official opposition is how the unemployed take the fund to the cleaners. The unemployment insurance fund provides employers with an opportunity to make changes in structure and lay-off people for a period of time and then recall them when they are ready. It is a subsidy situation for the corporation, more than the rip-off situation for the hundreds of thousands of people collecting unemployment insurance benefits that the hon. member for Hamilton West would have us believe.
The second aspect of the bill which we find objectionable is this disqualification of workers who quit jobs "without just cause," or who refuse "suitable employment" or who are "discharged". This is going to be a bureaucratic delight. I have had a very difficult time getting a definition for such phrases as "without just cause", "suitable employment" and "discharged", from the unemployment insurance office. What is "just cause"? There are examples of people who have been given a three-week disqualification period by the Unemployment Insurance Commission and in almost every instance these persons are the unorganized. Organized workers have grievance procedures and the benefit of union officials who are well acquainted with this very confusing act and the regulations. The unorganized people do not have this kind of help and invariably they suffer as a result of such disqualification.
I always thought that in our system you were innocent until proven guilty. At the present time, the bureaucracy slaps on the three-week disqualification and then a person may appeal and go through the board of referees, but if they are unorganized they have to get the permission of the board of referees' chairman before they can go to the umpire. Let us take the case of Miss "X", where an employer demanded to know the dates of her menstrual cycle. She refused to discuss the matter with him, and he told her to leave. That is just one incident. There is another one of a waitress behind the counter, and when the boss passes, his hands are too free so she quits.

That is right. But my point is that they apply the disqualification first and then you have to prove "just cause". How does one prove that? It is the woman's word against the employer's word. Whose word does the bureaucracy take? Certainly not the woman's. They would just say she was one of those women who worked for eight weeks and then wanted to collect benefits. That is the kind of mentality that permeates the UIC bureaucracy. It actually happens that the disqualification is imposed first and then the worker has to prove that it is in fact "just

cause". What is "just cause"? It is very difficult to prove. The bureaucracy has had a heyday with it.
Also, the phrase "suitable employment"-there is terminology to delight the bureaucrats. The definition of "suitable employment" may be very clear to those at the top, but when it gets down to the level of bureaucracy that deals with the public, it takes on colour depending upon who is interpreting it. The government says the proposed change to six weeks is due to the alarmingly high number of persons leaving their employment. In the white paper that the government issued with the amendments, it says that "despite high rates of unemployment and low ratios of job vacancies to the number of unemployed workers, the number of persons leaving their employment without good cause and refusing suitable employment remain at alarmingly high levels."
The figures indicate that 250,000 people quit their jobs in 1974. That is 2.5 per cent of the labour force. I should like further information on that. Surely it is important to know why they quit and in what sectors of the economy these quittings occurred. Most likely, the people included are some who have been referred to Denison Mines at Elliot Lake, and when they saw the conditions and learned of the impact of silicosis and the measures both levels of government have taken to clean it up, they refused the job and now are included in the 250,000 figure.
The minister is throwing around these figures to justify his argument. I suppose this and the other bill before the House with respect to cutting back the government's contributions in any increased cost of the medicare program could be termed law and order amendments. He is making a big pitch that the government is going to tighten up the Unemployment Insurance Act, when what it is doing is coming down hard on those people who can least defend themselves. They do not belong to a union and have no procedure for expressing dissatisfaction for their working conditions. They do not have the benefit of counselling, so have no option but to quit.
Most non-union workers do not bother to appeal a disqualification. First of all, the appeal is probably heard miles away from where they live and, secondly, the language of the notice from the unemployment insurance office, the significance of the regulations and everything about them, is very confusing and the unemployed feel threatened. When they phone the UIC office there is no one there to help them prepare an appeal. Even though the Unemployment Insurance Commission thinks that the appointment of some kind of ombudsman to help people prepare an appeal is a good idea, it has not appointed one. Further, if the unorganized worker loses an appeal to the board of referees, he cannot go to the umpire unless he first gets the permission of the chairman of the board of referees. On the other hand, we well know that in the case of organized workers the appeal goes automatically to the umpire.
[DOT] <1700)
Clearly, the bill discriminates against those who are unorganized. Do we want to force those who are unemployed and unorganized to accept dangerous jobs, to accept frustrating and low paying jobs? It seems to me that the minister is delivering these workers to those
kinds of employers who pay the minimum wage or less than the minimum-whose working conditions are less than safe! He is locking these workers into such jobs because they will need to wait for six weeks, if disqualified, plus an additional two weeks waiting period. This means that those people will be without benefits for two months, if they become unemployed under the conditions of this Bill C-69.
I suggest that the act of 1971 was more flexible. It provided more support to those who were working. The virtue of that act was this: it forced employers to improve working conditions of workers who were not happy because of long hours or low pay. It forced certain employers to do what is done in other sectors of the economy where there are proper working conditions and fair rates of pay. It seems to me that was one of the good aspects of the 1971 act.
What has the minister done now? I know what was at the back of his mind. I know the sort of advice he was getting. I remember what happened during the last election, when he attended a so-called great big meeting at Chelmsford arena in Nickel Belt. I know who came to see him.

This fellow was incensed because workers could get more on unemployment insurance than by working for him. He said that the Unemployment Insurance Act worked as a disincentive to work. So he came to his father confessor the minister over there, and told him about the problem. He said that he wanted to pay workers $2.50 an hour and determine conditions covering meals and living conditions, etc. Father confessor listened and listened, and the result is this legislation. Surely he knows that some of these fellows, some of these employers, impose on their workers the very worst working conditions it is possible to imagine Yet here he is bringing forward this kind of bill.
