speechtext: You mean, he is a friend of the employers?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I suppose he is. It is interesting to note that the government has not moved to increase the federal minimum wage. Oh, we have heard the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) promising that the government will consider raising the federal minimum wage. So far, it has not gone up. In relation to average industrial income, it has gone down. Between July, 1970, and July, 1975, the federal minimum wage increased by 58 per cent. In the same period, earnings in manufacturing increased by 70 per cent. Therefore, it seems to me that the government is ensuring a large pool of lowly paid workers for employers. These workers must work to support their families. We are providing many employees to employers who are not prepared to institute improved working conditions and fair rates of pay.
The other aspect of this bill my party finds objectionable is that amendment dealing with the dependency rate

October 27, 1975

of benefit. At present, the act provides for 75 per cent of the weekly wage to a claimant with dependants, and 66% per cent to a claimant without dependants. This bill contemplates eliminating the 75 per cent dependency rate and allowing only the 66% per cent, the rationale being that the government has introduced all sorts of programs for the benefit of families and that the claims for dependants can therefore be eliminated.
I happened to be looking at some documents and, lo and behold, I found a 1972 memo entitled "Some background notes on the unemployment insurance program." The memo set forth arguments to justify the then proposed dependency rate. The argument used then could be equally used now to justify the retention of the dependency benefit. The memo read in part:
Studies indicated that the benefit structure should permit the unemployed worker to meet at least non-deferable expenses while in search of new work. Economists estimated that about one third of a family's expenses could be deferred for a short time and it is for this reason that benefit payments in the initial stages of the program are set at two thirds of a claimant's average weekly earnings.
In the later stages, benefits can be raised to 75 per cent of average earnings if the claimant had dependants, because non-deferable expenses become more critical if unemployment persists.
As well, the low income groups, i.e. those earning $50 a week or less at the time they become unemployed, are permitted the dependency rate from the outset of their claim in recognition of their lesser capability to absorb a drop in income.
That argument is still valid, yet the minister has seen fit to eliminate the dependency benefit. That is a regressive move designed, I suggest, to make it difficult for unorganized workers to jump from job to job in the areas of Canada suffering from a slowdown in economic growth despite DREE programs and other programs which effectively accelerate technological change and increase profits but do little to create jobs.
The other amendment we cannot accept is the reduction in age from 70 years to 65 years of those eligible to pay UIC premiums and to receive UIC benefits. So far we have talked strictly about how this bill relates to people, to the unemployed. You cannot just consider statistics, whether there are 5,000 people of 65 or over who are unemployed, 100 such people, or only one person. If the bill discriminates against anyone 65 or over, it discriminates against all. Of course, the minister said that the government had considered benefits available under the Canada Pension Plan, old age security provisions and supplementary benefits to this age group are quite adequate. Do not forget, Madam Speaker, that two-thirds of working Canadians are not in unions. Hence, they do not participate in pension plans. Organized workers contribute to pension plans. Sometimes the employer only makes the contributions on behalf of the workers. As any economist will tell you, any worker who is not organized and who therefore does not participate in some kind of pension plan cannot quit work at age 65. It is not a matter of whether such workers want to work. The fact is that such workers must continue working. All our old age programs, supplementary benefit programs and what-have-you provide no more than $3,000, at maximum.
What is the poverty level in this country? It is approximately $4,800. The minister says they have given us the
Adjournment Motion
Canada Pension Plan and the old age supplement program, so we should be satisfied and get off their backs. That is not good enough. As I pointed out, for many 65 year olds, retirement is not a matter of taking your ease at the summer cottage or in a condominium in Florida. For many, it is a matter of economics. They do not continue working because they like it.
How many people do we know who have marked off the day of their retirement? I know many workers in my community who have marked the days on the calendar up to the date of their retirement. There are others who must still be available for work. Those people will be eliminated from the UIC rolls. All they can hope for is a low paying job that younger Canadians with higher expectations will not accept.
Even the three-week retirement benefit has gone out the window. In some companies, a person eligible for retirement at age 68 cannot get the three-week retirement benefit. This particular aspect of the bill discriminates against the elderly who are poor. This is a miserly, miserable, mean and insensitive proposal by the minister.
The minister represents a part of Canada where there is a great deal of unemployment-northern Ontario. There are a great many of these cases in his area. I am surprised that he is asking this House and this party to support Bill C-69. We on this side are not prepared to support it. We will fight against the bill as hard as we can. Our difference with the minister on this question is different from the position taken by the official opposition, which is that this bill should possibly be tightened up even more with still more people being cut off the unemployment rolls.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with some apprehension that I speak on the bill introduced this afternoon. I carefully listened to the minister and having known him for many years as an honest and just man, I was wondering what he was really thinking while making his statement. I am sure that if the minister had drafted the bill himself, it would be completely different, that is more much human and just. It would be a bill where the financial considerations would surely not override the human factors. However, what can you expect, like everybody else the minister is struggling in our false and so-called democratic system, while we live under an omnipresent bureaucracy headed by a technocracy serving financial powers which still allow us to live in Canada for a few years. That is why I want the minister to know that my remarks are more directed at the system than at himself, for I hold him in high esteem.
Before dealing with Bill C-69, An Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, we must keep in mind that the purpose of this bill is to lighten the burden of small wage-earners. It is quite the opposite, since this bill stems from the fifth great element in the program of the former Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to limit public involvement in connection with unemployment insurance. If I make this statement in my opening remarks, it is to caution my readers not to fall for the misleading representations in the act which, it so happens, reads:
Recommendation
His Excellency the Governor General has recommended to the House of Commons the present measure to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 to add, in the manner provided, a new class to the existing classes of insurable employment; to provide, in the manner prescribed, for changes in qualifying periods, benefit periods, entitlement to benefits and, rates of benefits; to provide, in the manner prescribed, for a new basis for the calculation that determines the proportion of the basic cost of benefit for a year that will be borne by the Government; to make the employer's premiums of Her Majesty in right of Canada payable by statute; and to provide for the payment of allowances to persons or their representatives who attend before an umpire on an appeal from a decision of the Minister.
All the newspapers which were probably well paid to publicize the fact that the federal government had finally decided to lead the way in reducing federal expenses have left out the fact that all of this would probably be achieved at the expenses of minimum wage workers. We must recognize that those who claim to keep the Canadian public well informed are unwilling or unable to admit that the victims of the example given by the federal government are those who earn $6,000 or less per year. And it is precisely to those unemployed that the minister is saying:
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
We have felt it necessary to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to give it more adaptability and fairness. The minister dares talk about justice when he proposes to cut off unemployment benefits to those who are 65 years of age or over, the very persons who have paid premiums right from the beginning of the unemployment insurance program and have never put in any claim. Why? We were told this afternoon that it was because old age pensions had been increased.
But, Madam Speaker, did he figure out that the higher old age pension fell far short of the cost of living increase since 1971. The minister dares speak of justice when he wants to raise the small wage earner's premiums. There are 5 per cent unemployed who earned only the minimum wage, that is $2.60 an hour in Quebec, without any possibility of indexation. Is it just to penalize a person with six weeks' waiting when a worker quits his job for personal reasons? Because it so happens, Madam Speaker, that a worker has personal reasons as is often the case when an employer discharges a worker. In my opinion, it is an injustice in the Russian manner. Is it just to give a claimant with one or more dependants only 66% when the old law was granting him 75 per cent, after the escalation of the cost of living due to the government's blunders and carelessness. To excuse the government, the minister talks of more generous family allowances. He very well knows that they are not making up the difference since 1971. He knows it but he cannot say it. It is merely social injustice which is reigning supreme since this government is in power and which they are mistaking for justice, because of their parliamentary majority.
I have stated before, with supporting evidence, that 80 per cent of the so-called social legislation passed through the House was clearly anti-social, and this bill is new proof of that. This bill is presented almost as a favour granted to people, a favour granted to the unemployed, like a bunch of flowers offered by a perfect valet. But looking at it more closely, what is it there to see, Madam Speaker? We bear in mind the minister's disconcerting promises of justice and equity, but the more deeply we examine the bill, the more we realize the discrimination which will result from it if no major amendment is moved before the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration. To illustrate more clearly my remarks, I will draw hon. members' attention to a few actual experiences which will highlight all the imposture hidden under this complacent literary style.
Take, for example, the question of illness and pregnancy. The bill provides for an increase or rather an extension of the period of coverage in case of illness or pregnancy. But if the minister keeps the same regulations, and that is the point, all diseases will be well codified and the officer's decisions will be mandatory. What will be the use of such an extension, then? If the regulations made by the bureaucrats who are now listening to me and approved by the minister without the reelected members of this House having a word to say and being even able to read them, determine, for instance, that an appendectomy requires three weeks' coverage, as though all surgery cases were similar, what will that extension mean? It all becomes a practical joke. Since 1971, we of the Social Credit Party
October 27, 1975

ask the government to acknowledge in priority the attending physician's diagnosis.
We are always confronted with a fait accompli, that is to say that the civil servant reverses the medical opinion to conform with he standards approved by the minister and the dictates of the bureaucracy.
Is there anything more antisocial and more ridiculous? Not one word dealing with that urgent problem is to be found in Bill C-69! The minister will object saying that the unemployed who is sick can always ask for a second, a third or even a fourth certificate. That is precisely what is ridiculous, Madam Speaker, since the surgeon or attending physician has stated that such and such a patient must rest for five, six or seven weeks, because of the seriousness of the operation and resulting convalescence. That this same doctor should have to sign two, three, four or even five certificates confirming the original prescription because a civil servant devoid of any medical knowledge has made a decision instead of the responsible person, the attending physician. Again the minister may object that some technocrats have done so or that the commission has its own physician.
Do you sincerely believe that the physician designated by the minister can appraise all the cases in his office in Montreal or elsewhere? There is nothing more ridiculous when civil servants say in such cases that it is Dr. Dunn's or someone else's decision. Let us put an end to this practical joke.
We, of the Social Credit, advise the minister to put forward an amendment so that the physician's diagnosis can only be reversed by an ad hoc medical board.
This afternoon I thought the minister would reduce the number of weeks for eligibility in case of illness, but he did nothing. People will still have to work for 20 weeks before being eligible for unemployment insurance benefits in case of illness. However, if there is a worker who needs money, it is the worker who is ill. The number of weeks for eligibility should be the same as for a worker in perfect health. The minister hinted that he would introduce further amendments and we hope that he will pay particular attention to the case I have just mentioned.
Another shortcoming in this bill is that it fails to mention anything new regarding entitlement to benefits nor does it set a limit date to establish entitlement in case of complications and dispute with the employer. It is the case when an employer refuses to pay for the stamps of an employee who has worked for several weeks for this employer, he then quits and goes to work for another boss who offers him higher wages and better working conditions.
I have solved several problems of this kind but it was only after forceful discussions and two or three months' waiting that I finally won the argument on behalf of the applicants. Let us sympathize over the plight of a bread winner who has to wait two or three months for his case to be settled. That, is a serious matter!
Right now, I still know another case which is pending, from which I infer either that officials do not receive clear instructions, or that they do not have the authority to settle on the spot the case of employers who are trying to punish workers for not accepting starvation wages.
Unemployment Insurance Act
The most peculiar thing in this case, which has been pending for a few months, is that civil servants believed the statements of the employer, his wife, his children, his whole family, while they seem to ignore completely the statements made under oath by the worker himself, his fellow workers and all those who cannot talk, when faced with dismissal. In brief, one accepts without hesitation the employer's statement and considers the worker as a liar when all his companions declare before the commission or the civil servants that he was actually doing such work during so many weeks, then the employer says no, because he was paying him cash every Saturday night. Those problems and tricks are found particularly in restaurants.
In my opinion, this problem should be considered by the government. That is why I wonder, Mr. Speaker, what brings the civil servants to deny so casually the statements made under oath by a worker against an employer's false statement. Maybe the unemployed will win his case. But this poor unemployed, who is sick to boot, has been waiting for more than two months and a half for the civil servants' decision. That is why we ask the minister to bring an amendment if necessary so that civil servants will have more authority to take actions vis-a-vis employers who fail to acknowledge the amount of time worked for them and to pay their employees the stamps for the weeks worked.
Madam Speaker, I had an unfortunate experience respecting hundreds of workers. This was another situation. All of them had been working for the Quebec Department of Lands and Forest. Only after action was taken against the Quebec government which had had the work classified as non-insurable employment by the Department of Revenue did all those workers win their case after waiting for a year. Only after a year was justice done to those workers employed by the government of Quebec. How is that for logic?
An amendment will therefore have to be introduced with respect to those governments in order to compel provinces to determine, before works start, whether such works, or workers will or will not be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits.
The bill does not deal either with lumberjacks-another serious problem in our parts-lumberjacks who are discriminated against as compared with other industrial workers. Indeed, if a lumberjack does not complete four weeks, the contractor has a right to give him no stamp at all, whereas in the rest of industry, if a worker is working for one, two or three weeks, he gets his stamps. Unscrupulous contractors can therefore take advantage of that measure by abusing it or even better by pestering the worker to have him leave the working site before completing the four weeks and therefore not qualify. Moreover, he gets disqualified for three weeks, and that disqualification will be extended to six weeks with the new bill. Do you know that in a whole winter, some contractors save hundreds of dollars through a form of legal injustice?
An amendment should be introduced to put the forest industry on equal footing with any other industry. We see every day that, contrary to the minister of manpower's own recommendations, the government appears to be acting unilaterally. They ignore representations by serious

October 27, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
bodies such as "Action-Chomage" in Montreal. I even wonder if bureaucrats in Ottawa took the time to read the latter's brief, otherwise Bill C-69 would be quite different.
I am referring here to claims for overpayment. Very often these overpayments are caused by ignorance of both statute and regulations. Even members of Parliament do not know these regulations, which are not submitted to them. How can workers find their way through that maze? The regulations are four times as bulky as the act itself, and they simply deprive the latter of any of its potentially good effects.
The government is proud of the $4 million of overpayment it got back. Who but the victims know of all the inequities caused by the exaction of forced declarations during house inquest, by threats of legal action or by intimidation. Over the last few years, the department doubled its army of inspectors sent to force declarations out of claimants. First, claimants were told they were being helped. Somebody came to their house, supposedly to help, and scribbled something on a piece of paper the claimant had to sign without any explanation, without any mention of consequences.
After these inquests, claimants received a benefit cancellation notice or a note of overpayment. The minister just admitted this afternoon that 144,000 unemployed were struck off the list in this way. Talk about a victory! There is a section on accounting errors. But there are also errors by omission, when the minister does not instruct his officials to explain the act and all the regulations, nor to fully inform workers and employers. There is a definite gap there.
It is ignorance of regulations on the part of both the employer and the worker. We say they are not allowed to ignore the law but, Madam Speaker, we are not allowed to ignore regulations yet they are not submitted to us, to this House for approval. And this is where the situation is serious. I think that you will obtain much more efficiency and honesty if you turn your staff into social workers instead of policemen looking for new victims that will only fill up the coffers of the government. The minister is not interested in giving justice to the unemployed, but only in boasting a fat unemployment insurance fund.
To this end, he will double the contributions if needed to have an unemployment insurance program financially self-sufficient. When the government grants almost half a million dollars to the CBC to hire actors at enormous salaries where is its concern about self-sufficiency? Yet the Unemployment Insurance Commsision has a social role to fulfill much more urgent than the CBC.
And, all those grants that the government allots for research or so-called manpower incentives-I could give you many examples of it-and that are nothing but political patronage. Let us not forget that all those selective grants are taken from the consolidated revenue fund, that is to say from the pockets and from the pay cheques of the workers. The minister had the honesty to admit it this afternoon.
The former Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said that it was necessary to change the way to calculate the part of unemployment insurance benefits financed by contribu-

tors. And he added that the cost of the program beyond the self-supported part was a burden for the state. The basis of his tabulations was then an unemployment rate of 4 per cent. But is it the workers' responsibility if unemployment has reached the present levels? Then why should the small earners support the burden of government mismanagement?
One only has to consider that in Quebec alone out of a labour force of 2,729,000 at the end of September only 2,476,000 workers were working, which means that 203,000 are unemployed. After all the increases in premiums and the restrictions on benefit payments, how does one dare talk about justice for workers? Is this really the time to restrict expenditures for unemployment insurance when we are facing the hardest winter in many years?
The minister was sincere when he admitted he agreed entirely with the principles of the unemployment insurance program. It provides, the former Minister of Finance used to say, a steady income to workers who are unfortunate enough to lose their jobs, and reduces the anxieties caused by unemployment. Well, I learned from certain bureaucrats that the new orders are that benefits are to be paid so the unemployed will look for work first.
I am under the impression that technocrats give orders to officials who must obey under penalty of tough sanctions although they are aware that those anticipated orders, to say the least, are in conflict with the very spirit of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
One may fool the public for a while, Madam Speaker, but not indefinitely. Today, the majority of workers have organized so they will not be bamboozled by the government. That is why we are not surprised to hear the protests of the leaders, the large unions, now able to detect all the double dealings hidden in a text of law. For example, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress stated that all small workers will bear the weight of the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act and confirmed that 75 per cent of all unemployment insurance claimants earn $6,000 a year.or less.
Madam Speaker, it seems to me the Unemployment Insurance Commission is a service to the public. What do we find out, after we have been promised two years ago that we would have independent offices in the riding of Roberval, offices where decisions could be taken on the spot in order to provide personal service to persons unemployed for 15 days at most?
What did we get? A limited staff whose only task is to receive complaints and refer them to the regional office. These poor officials are there only to hear the complaints and often the insults voiced by unemployed people who have had it up to here, simply because those officials have no decision power. On two occasions, I was nevertheless promised that everything would be settled, but we are still waiting for those services.
Far be it from me to put the blame on the regional office which is overworked and cannot therefore give adequate service. Anyway, the persons responsible for that office look forward to the day when the minister will finally decide to give the services asked for many months ago.
Madam Speaker, there are many other points with which I should like to deal, such as the four weeks without
October 27, 1975

benefits, for instance, but my time is running short. I want to ask the minister to read my remarks carefully and then, to introduce himself the required amendments to this House, if he really wants, as he said again this afternoon, to treat the unemployed fairly.
As a consolation prize, the minister tells us that in the future he will issue a new insurance number to those who have lost theirs. I believe this is already current practice because it has happened several times in my riding: I had no trouble getting another number for those people who had problems with their numbers.
Madam Speaker, those who are entitled to benefits and were denied those rights by decisions of civil servants can finally have their travelling expenses paid, when they will have to appear before the board of referees, while they used to pay all their expenses. In future, I am pleased to see that the minister has announced this slight improvement which is not much. Last year, I think that at least ten of my constituents had to refer to arbitration. Thus, very little is granted, only peanuts!

speakeroldname: Mrs. Iona Campagnolo (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think it is indeed a unique occasion when members of this House can speak on an unemployment insurance bill because it seems to me that most members of parliament spend a good deal of time assisting constituents through the sometimes intricate maze that is dependent upon their getting their benefits through that commission. As a result of the comprehensive review of that act, certain complexities and inequities have become very apparent. That is what Bill C-69 has come to grips with now.
For almost two years unemployment insurance has been the subject of comprehensive review to determine whether it continues to meet its mandate in the most effective way possible in a dynamic modern economy. A number of complexities and inequities have come to light through the four years of experience which are now on record with the act, and through the results of the review.
One important inequity which has been brought forward relates to a degree of rigidity in the maternity benefits provided under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act. The 1971 act limited the payment of maternity benefits to a set 15-week period, with eight weeks immediately preceding the week of confinement and six weeks following it. This called for a very precise estimate of the date of birth by a woman's physician and took little account of the vagaries of nature. Thus women often lost several weeks of benefit if the birth of their child was either premature, or miscalculated. Thus the spirit of the provision of maternity benefits through the Unemployment Insurance Commission was often frustrated by a simple matter of biology.
Unemployment Insurance Act
I should like to make particular reference to those women of northern and less populous areas who must often arrange to leave their homes in advance of a birth in order to bear their child in a modern medical facility. There was no differential possible in the previous legislation for such circumstances, circumstances which often cost them considerable loss of benefits not lost by their southern sisters.
We made the elimination of this inequity part of the omnibus bill, C-16, on which I was privileged to speak on May 29 in this House. That bill, which received Royal Assent on July 30, will be implemented the first week of February 1976, and its provisions will provide a measure of flexibility to maternity benefits which will guarantee that the mother will receive the full benefit to which she is entitled, without placing her unborn child on notice to be born on a pre-ordained Unemployment Insurance Commission schedule.
V50)
There have been inequities evident in the provision of sickness benefits as well, and a similar degree of flexibility will be introduced into the payment of these benefits by Bill C-69. Under the present legislation, sickness benefits are only payable during the first 15 weeks of a claim for which benefits are payable. As a result, a person who has been on claim for some weeks and then falls ill and becomes incapable of working must face either a much reduced eligibility for sickness benefits, or in some cases may find himself without any protection at all at a time when it is most desperately needed.
Bill C-69 proposes to redress this inequity by making sickness benefits payable for a maximum of 15 weeks during all initial periods of a claim that has been established. Thus, instead of limiting these benefits to the first 15 weeks for which benefits are payable, they may now be payable during the first 25 compensable weeks which may be paid at any time during the first 39 weeks of a claim. This almost doubles the degree of flexibility for sickness benefits and is expected to resolve a problem encountered by many claimants, one which has proved a real hardship for far too many Canadians.
A related problem, and one which my constituents have drawn to my attention on a number of occasions, relates to the fact that claimants may not under the present act terminate their claim, even when it is in their own interest to do so. This is particularly important in the case of special benefits, such as sickness and maternity, which are only payable in the initial stages of the claim. For example, claimants who draw several weeks of benefit, return to work for 20 or more weeks, and then fall ill, find themselves ineligible to receive sickness benefits because they are out of the initial benefit period of their claim. Bill C-69 will permit such claimants to terminate their existing claim and establish a new one on the basis of the 20 or more weeks that they worked, thus enabling them to establish eligibility for special benefits.
Prior to 1971 the Unemployment Insurance Act contained a provision allowing claimants who had been out of the labour market involuntarily to be granted an extension in their qualifying period so that they could have the protection of unemployment insurance during the crucial
8586

October 27, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
period of their re-entry into the work force. For example, persons who had been working in insurable employment and then fell ill for a year or more so that they could not work, or who were incarcerated in a penal institution, could have their qualifying period extended to enable them to establish eligibility for benefits once they were ready to return to the work force.
The 1971 legislation reduced the qualifying period to the point where people needed only eight weeks of insurable employment in the preceding 52, or since their last claim, to become eligible for benefits. It was thought that the eight week period would be short enough to allow people who had been out of the work force to re-establish their eligibility quickly. Unfortunately, however, experience shows that despite this easing of the qualifying conditions, situations still exist where persons are unable to qualify for benefits because of a lengthy absence from the active labour force. Bill C-69 proposes to extend the qualifying period to 104 weeks from the current 52 for persons in these unique situations who are actively seeking to reestablish themselves in the productive sphere of living by earning the means to pay their way.
In addition to extending the qualifying period, the bill also proposes to extend the benefit period for such people. That means that people who have established a claim for benefit and then lose their eligibility because of an involuntary withdrawal from the work force will be able to qualify for an extension of their benefit period when they are ready to seek employment again.
Groups which will benefit from this proposal include claimants on approved training courses, persons who are incapable of working for reasons of sickness or disability, those who receive temporary workmen's compensation, and inmates of penal institutions.
I do not know why it was at that point that I suddenly thought of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), but the hon. member really aroused my curiosity to a high degree when he mentioned that family allowance was for the children. I wondered if he really did give family allowance cheques to his children. I think the government made a very wise decision when it decided who the trustee for family allowance would be. It is the wife, not the husband, and with good reason, because allowances are issued for the benefit of the family and not as pin money in lieu of allowances. This is done by thousands and thousands of wise and thrifty women across this country.
Under the present act persons working on local initiatives and assistance program projects are eligible for employment insurance coverage. However, the project sponsors, that is, those who develop and obtain funding for projects and who often supervise the projects, spearheading them in many ways toward realization, these spark plugs, if you will, Madam Speaker, are not eligible. This is an inequity which this bill proposes to redress. This proposal is in support of the importance which the federal government is placing on job training, in particular on LEAP and LIP which have, from their inception, actively encouraged the participation of the unemployed in the creation and management of labour intensive projects.
The historic reason for criticism of LIP and LEAP escapes me, but I think it must be because so many members of the House are representatives of large urban

areas, and in those areas which are not gigantic cities LIP and LEAP have become a veritable touchstone of improvement in small places. They are visible and tangible assets to them. In non-urban areas of Canada you can look at recreation centres erected where they would never be erected any under any other program; you can look at the finishing of housing, at the erection of fire halls, and the establishment of senior citizens' help programs. I inspected one yesterday in the Queen Charlotte Islands. It was one that our federal and B.C. governmental agencies considered and said was impossible because it would cost probably $1 million, so of course it could not be done. It is an erosion control system which keeps the Pacific ocean from eroding village land. The people there put out a LIP project and during the first phase for a mere $27,000, with some voluntary and some paid work, have begun to make this possible.
I would like to continue, Madam Speaker, but I see it is six o'clock, so I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saint-Jean (Mr. Smith), that the debate now be adjourned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I was in Regina-Lake Centre last week. I found that a lot of people there are unemployed. Therefore I am sure the hon. member appreciates LIP projects as I do.
There has been concern expressed about the appeal system. The appeal system is an integral part of the whole unemployment insurance plan. It has been in existence since 1941, providing an effective recourse for both claimants and employers.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) talked today very knowingly about the sweet little waitress who had the misfortune of having a boss who put his hands where they should not be. He forgets there is legal
recourse for this kind of thing. Most of the women I know would not be above putting him in his place, going to court and getting a successful judgment against the offender and claiming their UIC benefits as a result.
Cases are heard by the Federal Court of Canada, the umpire if you will. I think "umpire" is a very good term. I think it puts succinctly what we were discussing earlier in this debate today. This is fed back into the eligibility determinations made by the commission. Thus the appeal system is crucial not only in terms of offering an effective channel through which to challenge bureaucratic decisions but also as keeping the program responsive and attuned to the judiciary's interpretation of the way the program should operate. And challenging bureaucratic decisions is a process which I am sure hon. members opposite are as happy to see as I am and, that includes members of the New Democratic Party.
An important amendment in Bill C-69 provides for the payment of travelling expenses by the UIC for its clients and their representatives attending hearings of the umpire in cases concerning coverage under the act. The legislation provides for the payment of expenses of appellants who are appealing cases concerning benefit. The proposed amendment increases the accessibility of the appeal system to persons who disagree with decisions of the commission.
I am sure members opposite who have small disagreements with the minister over this bill will bring them to the fore in the committee.
I think I would be really remiss in winding up this discussion tonight were I to do so without saying how much I appreciate the efforts of those in the field who administer the present legislation and who will administer Bill C-19 when it becomes an act. These are the men and women who deal day after day with the ordinary people we are supposed to represent here. We hear all too often from members opposite that there is nothing but a giant bureaucracy out there with no feeling for human beings. It is our job to make sure this is not the case. If the people at the bureaucratic level fail it is because we have failed to bring the message to them, and that is what I am asking you to do tonight. It is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that the U.I.C. people in the field, who are dealing with the conflicts and human problems are faced every day by many people in this country, some of whom never dreamed they would ever be out of a job-they felt they were beyond the pale, that they would never need to call upon the resources of the country to protect them. More and more they find that this, indeed, can happen, and I would like especially to remember those who deal with them on a day to day basis.
