subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a most timely opportunity to talk about Bill C-69, a bill with unemployment insurance, because we are at almost the same time dealing with inflation and discussing inflation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) suggested last weekend that union leaders who do not obey guidelines might well be put in jail in order to help the process.
I should like to quote something about the attitude of the public as stated by R. S. Malone in the Globe and Mail
October 27, 1975

of today, Monday, October 27. Speaking of inflation he had this to say:
But what about some of the larger and even more "untouchable" items? What about the staggering annual costs in unemployment benefits? All Canadians are aware that this program has become a national scandal to which Ottawa closes its eyes. Surely a time has come to bring a halt to the massive cheating and moonlighting which goes on, costing the taxpayers millions a month.
Some strict screening, individual investigation, regular monthly reviews, effective penalties and allowance cuts when reasonable work is refused, are long overdue.
This may be an extreme view but it is typical of the view held by many among the public. On the other hand of course, we, as members of parliament, tend to come into contact with many cases in which there appear to be an element of injustice following the application of unemployment insurance regulations.
As one who was involved with the legislation in 1971, I think I can say that as a result of the changes which were made then the whole plan was removed farther away from the concept of a general insurance plan. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, the most important aspect of this legislation is the change being made in the bench mark rather than the regulations we have been discussing.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey), when he was minister of labour, had this to say when he brought forward his white paper:
The government is not only willing to help provide a system of income support during an adjustment process; it is also ready to assume the cost of extra unemployment insurance benefits when the national unemployment rate exceeds 4 per cent. This policy is perhaps one of the most interesting in the entire proposal It clearly establishes the government's responsibility for the financial support of a national unemployment insurance program over and above the self-financing aspect.
With this change in the guidelines and the bench marks it is quite obvious the government has changed the whole goal of unemployment insurance. Now, as time goes on, bringing us into a moving average of the previous eight years of employment, within a few years employers and employees will be paying almost the full shot and, in turn, the government will be making the rules by which the money is spent. It seems to me important that we decide whether we are running a reasonable insurance program, or whether we are running a social welfare or social benefit program. If it is an insurance program then it is probably fair and reasonable that the employers and employees should pay for it. If it is a social welfare program surely the government of the day, the public exchequer, is the agency which must take a hand in it and put up a lot of the money.
What about the philosophy behind unemployment insurance? At first glance social justice should be the principal supporting argument in favour of unemployment insurance. It appears unfair that those least capable of bearing the burden of unemployment and least responsible for its causes, should suffer hardship. It might be felt, too, that productivity would increase because of an increased feeling of security among workers. Superficially, at least, unemployment seems to conform to the tests of an insurable risk: it applies to a sufficiently large group of people and over a sufficiently wide range of operations to permit the operation of the law of averages, and, theoretically, the economic loss can be compensated for, wholly or partially,
Unemployment Insurance Act
by indemnifying an idle worker on the basis of former earnings.
It should be noted that voluntary unemployment insurance plans, widely prevalent in Europe in the early part of this century, broke down because they were not actuarially sound. The same can now be said of our own unemployment insurance system. Further, in the event of major calamity or depression, the strain of cyclical unemployment of a severe sort will lead to the complete collapse of our way of handling payments to the unemployed. To some extent this has happened causing the federal treasury to step in.
There are certain inherent features which are detrimental to the unemployment insurance concept. In circumstances of severe unemployment the fund is likely not great enough to carry the excess load, and even if an enormous reserve were to be accumulated its sudden disposal on the money market would depress business.
There are bound to be all kinds of bad side effects attached to any unemployment insurance program. The contributions of employees tend to increase costs and prices, and the contributions of employers lead to increased wage demands. Then, too reliance on unemployment insurance in times of need curtails the incentive to save. This reduces savings which are necessary for our economy to prosper. The unemployment insurance program is detrimental to employees' loyalty and increases labour turnover. As well, the psychological side effects of unemployment insurance are harmful. Work is increasingly looked upon as being purely optional instead of being viewed as a vital necessity in order to survive.
Unemployment insurance promotes evasion of responsibility; governments turn a blind eye to all kinds of abuses; workers believe they have only rights, no duties; and employers are given no incentive to maintain employment. A true insurance program would have to offer financial rewards to employees who would build up credit in the form of reduced premiums by not applying for unemployment insurance payments, and to employers who maintain payrolls and do not lay off employees unnecessarily.
It is obvious now that there must be a recognition of the key here: "Unemployment exists", according to John Maynard Keynes, "because employers are deprived of profit". Therefore the only real improvement in the unemployment situation lies in preventing unemployment, not in expedience for distributing the loss occasioned by it. Obviously compassion and justice require assistance for those truly in need. By and large the working public would gladly support any such proposal.
Having given some thought to what pitfalls are in a truly insurance proposal, we may follow along to discuss some of the changes that occurred in 1971 when the new Unemployment Insurance Act was brought forward.
It is obvious that the government miscalculated when it brought forward this proposal. As one who was on the committee I might say that the government was obviously flying blind. It did not know or have any reasonable concept of what the cost of the program would be in the years to come. At that time the unemployment pay-out

October 27, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
was based on 43 per cent of the average worker's income, and rising as high as 50 per cent in certain cases.
The minister in charge of the unemployment insurance legislation and his officials obviously had no real forecast of what the expenditures would be. First of all they were presented with evidence to show that there would be a shortfall of at least $350 million, a minimum figure based on conditions existing in the year ending March 31, 1970, when unemployment was 4.8 per cent. The government made errors in its calculations and concluded there would only be an increase in the pay-out rate from 43 per cent to 66% per cent of the income of claimants generally, ignoring the fact that there would be a considerable cost in the form of additional benefits during the phase calling for 75 per cent of income.
The government did not calculate that the ceiling benefit of $53 a week then would increase to $100 per week under the new amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Furthermore the government proposed that the waiting period be extended from one to two weeks. The unemployment insurance people estimated this change would give rise to a saving in benefits of $160 million. That figure was impossible. It did not take into account that following the two weeks waiting period that the claimant would be paid three weeks's benefits. The only ceiling that would arise in this case was where a new job was found within the two weeks, but the white paper acknowledges that normally this takes from three to five weeks.
No allowance has been made for an obvious increase in benefit costs that would occur as a result of the shortened eligibility period of eight weeks. Certainly this is considered to amount to more that $65 million.
At that time facts and figures in respect of unemployment insurance in the 1970's were presented to the parliamentary committee. Following the estimate of what the cost of unemployment insurance would be in 1975 at a rate of 7 per cent, the estimate then based on 1972 figures would bring this to $1,081 million.
We have now an unemployment rate of only slightly more than 7 per cent; 7.2 per cent to 7.5 per cent, yet the cost of unemployment insurance is $4 billion. Even allowing for an increase in the average weekly wage from the $150 in 1970 to something like $200 now, the government's estimate was not even close. If its estimate had been accurate, the cost of unemployment insurance this year would be something in the neighbourhood of $1,500 million, a far cry from the $4 billion it is actually costing us. Never mind what happened to the fellow with the fishes and the loaves feeding the multitude. No one could have been more wrong than the unemployment officials and the minister in estimating the cost which has now reached $4 billion.
In the intervening period the minister kept saying there would not be an increase in the cost. It is perhaps difficult to relate unemployment insurance costs to the general economy because of the rapid inflation and the variation in the unemployment rate. It is difficult to relate this in constant dollars. We can only look back and compare it with what has gone before. Perhaps it would be beneficial to make a comparison between our gross national product at the market price and unemployment pay-outs. This might be illuminating and of some value.

For instance in 1964 the gross national product was about $50 billion and the unemployment insurance pay-out was $324 million, or 0.65 per cent. That percentage pay-out held fairly steady during the 1960's. In 1965 it was 0.57 per cent of the gross national product, in 1967 it was 0.54 per cent, in 1968 it was 0.61 per cent, in 1970 it was 0.82 per cent, and in 1971 it was 0.95 per cent. Then we came to 1972 when it suddenly jumped to 1.81 per cent. In other words, with the change to the Unemployment Insurance Act we had a doubling of the pay-out under the unemployment insurance fund in comparison to the gross national product. This has increased until at the present time we have a pay-out of nearly $1 billion and our gross national product is estimated at approximately $140 billion, or 2.92 per cent.
There has obviously been a fundamental change in respect of unemployment insurance. Some might suggest that the additional people brought in under the act in 1971 made the difference, but certainly these people would not normally be unemployed then or now. This includes government workers, federal, provincial and municipal, and certainly government workers are not usually unemployed. In fact a government employee almost has to be guilty of moral turpitude to be discharged.
Teachers were brought in, but I am sure they would not increase the unemployment rate. I think most members will have found it is almost impossible for a teacher to collect unemployment insurance. Employees of hospitals and charitable institutions were covered. Perhaps there might have been a slight increase in respect of workers in lower skilled jobs, but those in highly skilled jobs, I am sure, did not contribute to the increase. It also covered the armed forces, police forces, and professional athletes. Surely those people have not changed the pattern of payout under unemployment insurance.
When questioning the minister who appeared before the committee on May 25, 1971, I asked:
Mr. Minister, I would just like clarification of this saving on the first week of $160 million, on that paper you kindly sent around.
Later I asked:
-by increasing the waiting period from one to two weeks, you are saving about 45 per cent of the regular unemployment, based on a 4 per cent rate.
MR. Mackasey: But the money is going elsewhere into the plan. We have increased benefits, we have lowered eligibility to the eight weeks, despite the two weeks. It is really a distribution on the table. As I recall, this table shows were we save and where we spend, and we show that we increase the costs by $65 million by lowering eligibility.
MR- Ritchie: Mr. Minister, what astounds me is that by increasing the waiting period from one to two weeks, you are saving about 45 per cent of the regular unemployment, based on a 4 per cent rate.
MR. Mackasey: Unemployment is really front-loaded. Even in the month of January this year, at the height of all that high unemployment, over 110,000 or 120,000 people went back to work.
At the time the government passed the Unemployment Insurance Act it had no concept of the cost of this program. Furthermore, there is intense feeling that unemployment insurance is a great rip-off and that people are collecting benefits unnecessarily, to the detriment of the working fabric of our enonomy. This may or may not be true, but I think it can be said that when benefits are available a worker is entitled to manage his affairs so as to obtain them if he so decides.
October 27, 1975

At a time of statistically high unemployment I was astounded to hear tonight of a riding that was awarded nearly $1 million in LIP grants which is based on the unemployment rate, while in my rural area riding the total was $155,000. One wonders how accurate are the unemployment statistics. At a time of statistically high unemployment workers are difficult to obtain for industry. There has been a lack of available workers, particularly in agricultural and other basic industries such as forestry and mining. This is particularly true in respect of jobs which are not too pleasant.
In some of these cases I do not think it is because sufficient money is not being offered. There may be many unemployed workers, but they are unemployed because they cannot find the particular jobs they would like to have. If the economy is to function, then the jobs which are not too pleasant must be filled. If we are to have a healthy and vigourous economy we might ask whether unemployment insurance contributes to this.
In respect of the Unemployment Insurance Act, and certainly its administration, it has been one of my contentions that the Unemployment Insurance Commission is unnecessarily severe in respect of certain people who are not protected through belonging to a large union or a large company. I cannot help but feel at times that in a rural area it is unnecessarily severe in administering regulations concerning small people who are not likely to be able to fight back. The cases brought to my attention always involve people who do not belong to a large union or a large corporation.
Many people in my area, in the small hamlets and villages, cannot obtain unemployment insurance benefits because the officials have ruled that they must move to work centres a good many miles away. The distance rule at times is being applied very severely, and sometimes I feel unfairly. For this reason I maintain that many people who pay unemployment insurance dues and live in rural areas in fact are virtually excluded from receiving benefits because of the residence rule. I do not know whether this is fair. Generally the unemployment insurance officers rule that they must go many miles away. This really is impracticable.
Indeed Unemployment Insurance officials today I say would depopulate many hamlets and villages by moving workers to larger urban centres. Obviously in order to control abuses of the fund the officials apply the regulations very severely. Unfortunately in my area they seem to apply them to the casual people and those least able to cope.
These people to whom I refer are doing jobs which no one else wants. They are farm labourers, camp cooks, and people who work away from home on road work. It seems to me that before this bill is passed we should recognize there should be a thorough-going inquiry into the working philosophy of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. What the government has proposed will not materially change the thrust of the Unemployment Insurance Act, other than shift it from a government role to a private role so far as paying for it is concerned. In fact, with the government still making the rules and regulations there will be a tendency on the part of politicians to increase benefits since the public treasury will not have to bear the
Unemployment Insurance Act
full cost. We need to know whether or not unemployment insurance is to be viewed in terms of true unemployment insurance, as income redistribution, or social welfare.
A recent publication of Statistics Canada gives an idea of what income redistribution has been in the country as a whole. I think this is quite interesting. For instance, for the month of July Newfoundland received $12 million in payments; New Brunswick received $11 million; Quebec received almost $95 million; Ontario received $80 million; Manitoba received $4 million; Saskatchewan received $3 million, Alberta almost $7 million, and British Columbia almost $32 million. When one examines these figures one finds a wide variation in the amount of money received relative to the population of each province. The total paid out was $256 million. Had it been paid out in Canada on the basis of Manitoba's insurance pay-out the total payment would have amounted to something like $88 million, while in respect of Saskatchewan it would have been even better at something like $70 million.
I ask what effect income redistribution has on the structure of our economy and our society. We have a very contrived country. The government works on rules which are based on political expediency rather than on the state of the market. So I think we should examine the effect redistribution has had on the growth of our country. We have paid out vast amounts of money in DREE and other grants to entice industry to backward areas or areas in which industries do not seem to thrive.
Does unemployment insurance aid and abet the failure of industries to establish and thrive in certain backward areas? Why should there be such a large discrepancy between one area and another? This is not entirely explained by the good or bad times which occur in our economy in selected regions, from time to time. Do the methods used in respect of employment vary from area to area? Do the criteria in respect of payment vary more in one area than in another? Certainly from my experience with unemployment insurance claims in my area I can say the officials could cause the spending or the saving of hundreds of millions of dollars in a year by applying the regulations severely or not so severely.
Does unemployment insurance encourage workers to remain unnecessarily in a high unemployment area? We must look at this particularly because of the extended benefits policy whereby a person with only eight weeks attachment to the labour force may receive benefits of up to 52 weeks if conditions are right.
We might look at the question of whether or not unemployment insurance benefits are too high at 66% per cent. We cannot blame any worker today who takes advantage of these benefits if it is in his interest to do so. If the system allows a payment then the worker is entitled to this payment. If the rate is 66% of a man's average weekly earnings, then particularly if he has a cold job in this cold country he may want to take advantage of it. His costs are increased if he has to buy extra clothes, or drive his car a long way and he is not able to start it in the freeze up. This is where the figure of 66% must be seriously considered.
In his recent budget the former minister of finance stated that unemployment insurance would be changed,

October 27, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
and he proposed five basic changes on the basis that the cost to the government is becoming unwieldy and that the present act contains undesirable features. He pointed out the fact that the act was too expensive in its operations, and that the present cost to the government is almost double the amount that the government had forecast in view of the rate of unemployment back in 1972. Benefit payments in 1975-76 are expected to exceed $3.75 billion, placing a total cost on the government of approximately $1.75 billion. This is cause for considerable alarm.
Unemployment in 1974 averaged 5.4 per cent and has been running this year at an annual rate of 7.2 per cent. It may well be that due to the state of the economy the rate of unemployment may well reach 8 per cent by the end of the year. But unemployment statistics do not account for all the increases in pay-outs. While unemployment benefits rose by 31 per cent from April, 1974, to April, 1975, the total cost of UIC rose 69 per cent. More important is the fact that the length of the benefit period for recipients increased by 51 per cent over the same period. In other words, people did not go back to work at the same rate as they did previously. This factor can be interpreted as the result of either the mismanagement of the unemployment insurance fund or a growing trend where people feel more secure collecting unemployment insurance benefits than working. Needless to say, the former minister of finance has tended to place the blame more on the latter than on the former.
With regard to disincentives let me say that I have not seen much evidence one way or another. In fact in a report put out by the Department of Manpower and Immigration entitled "Canadian Work Values" the following conclusion is stated clearly:
Clearly, Canadians are committed to work- Canadians see themselves as industrious people to whom work contributes a feeling of success and, for a large proportion, of personal fulfilment.
While this is a fact, it is true that more and more people confine themselves to work which they like. This is human, it is what we would all like to do, namely, work at jobs we feel we like. But in practice all sectors of our economy must be covered and some people must do jobs which they do not find too interesting.
I should now like to discuss briefly some of the solutions the government has proposed. First, the government proposes an increase from three to six weeks in the period of disqualification for those who have quit or been fired from their jobs, or have refused suitable employment. Superficially one cannot critize this proposal, but certainly I feel strongly that certain people who leave their jobs, who quit or who are fired, do so for good reason. We all have personality problems. Very often it is not the boss who is the reason for a person quitting his job, it is his fellow workers or some difficult situation, perhaps a personal situation. Therefore, it seems to me there is place here for providing some recourse for the one who is fired or who quits if the reason for his quitting was beyond his control.
The second government proposal is that the payments of premiums and the receipt of benefits will terminate at age 65. Again it seems to me that the government is saying to people 65 and over, "We do not want you in the labour force any longer". Perhaps due to the high rate of unemployment this can be tolerated at present, but we are fast

approaching an era in which we will need those who are 65 and over in our work force.
In other societies in Europe and in Russia people over 65 years of age are wanted in the work force. It would seem to be practical that some arrangements be made to allow these people to collect unemployment insurance if they wish. Many people over that age do not want to work because they have worked a lifetime and they do not want to continue. But I believe that within reason we should encourage people over 65 to remain in the labour force, and especially those people who do not draw unnecessarily on the fund should be allowed to continue. Perhaps one solution might be to give them an option of whether or not they draw on unemployment insurance.
I would like to make a few comments now on the new government employee adjustment procedure. Unemployment insurance currently operates on the basis of employee-employer contributions covering costs when unemployment is 4 per cent or less. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) stated to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration on May 27, 1975:
An unemployment scheme like ours does have a crucial role to play in keeping the economy ship afloat in an industrialized country and that is something that we should recognize when we examine the cost of a program like this one of ours.
What the government is proposing is a fundamental change. By changing the 4 per cent unemployment benchmark to an eight year moving average, and by doing so during a recession, the government is ensuring that little or none of the additional cost of unemployment insurance, which accrues from its inability to deal with unemployment, will fall on the federal treasury in years ahead. Since this renegation of the clearly established benchmark of 1971 makes it apparent that the government is no longer committed to 4 per cent unemployment, and since a great need exists for unemployment insurance, irrespective of the government's posture, it is safe to assume that the total cost of unemployment insurance will remain exorbitant and probably will even increase.
I should like to read to you what the present Postmaster General, the former minister of labour, had to say when he was giving evidence on 25 June, 1971, before the Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration. He said:
. .. The point I was making ... which is a valid one, I think, is that if we had no unemployment insurance plan, or if the government was not seized under this bill with the responsibility of providing the features beyond the 4 per cent, despite Mr. Thomas' arguments, which were good arguments, in that event governments would have to assume their legal and moral responsibility to reward the unemployed in this country. If you had a 10 per cent period for instance of unemployment at 7 per cent you would certainly have an added burden on the general revenue or on the Treasury to provide some financial assistance to people.
In other words, the minister of that day was adamant that the 4 per cent was necessary, that the country had a social obligation to shoulder the burden, and that it would be a good thing because it would provide the government with an incentive to reduce unemployment. Now, however, the burden created by the ineptitude of the government will fall directly on the shoulders of the taxpayer through what is in fact a new form of payroll taxation, and at that, regressive taxation of the worst ilk.
October 27, 1975

This may have been quoted previously, but Don McGil-livray, a financial analyst writing for the Financial Times, wrote the following:
. .. the change in unemployment insurance financing faces Canadian employees and employers with an additional tax burden at least twice as heavy as the extra tax on gasoline ... this extra payroll tax under the new formulae may reach $800 million to $1 billion next year.
The important thing is that this is merely a transfer of tax from the federal treasury to the employee and the employer, but is it in effect a scheme of viable insurance, or does it carry a large element of welfare? Employers and employees would be reasonably happy to carry a scheme which is a true insurance program, but when it is a welfare scheme or where there is a large element of welfare involved, surely it becomes the decision of the government of the day to modify it as to what pattern they shall pay.
Leaving aside the points which have been debated, the important thing is the changing of the bench mark which reduces the cost to the government and increases the cost to employers and employees, while in effect the same pay-outs and the same difficulties remain in the system.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Arthur Portelance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have great pleasure in taking part in this important debate on Bill C-69.
This most important bill was tabled for first reading on July 8,1975, and I hope that, with the cooperation of all members of this House, it will be passed without a deljy which might impede the application of measures designed to provide more efficient administration for the Unem-plc^nent Insurance Commission.
Since 1940, thousands of Canadians have taken advantage of this program, but it was not until 1971 that workers have been granted an unprecedented protection when benefits passed from 40 per cent of their weekly earnings to 66% per cent.
Previously, if a worker was so unfortunate as to become ill, he could not receive any benefits under the act. An applicant had to accumulate 30 weeks out of the last 104 to be entitled to benefits, which according to several members of all parties in the House, made the policy outdated and discriminatory for thousands of Canadian workers. And especially those who live in areas where the unemployment rate is higher, such as in the Maritimes, in Quebec or some locations in the prairies or Ontario. Therefore the 1971 legislation compensated for several injustices, reducing to eight the number of weeks required to qualify for some benefits and to twenty weeks for all benefits such as the allowance in the case of illness or maternity and granting a maximum of 51 weeks of benefits.
It is therefore obvious that the new unemployment insurance scheme is fairer and more efficient and allows a better distribution of incomes than before 1971. However, Mr. Speaker, since the coming into force of the new legislation, several members, especially in the government caucus, have made representations and recommendations to have the unemployment insurance legislation amended
Unemployment Insurance Act
to correct some problems which according to them create injustices for workers who are disallowed benefits for some rather technical reasons as well as the problem due to abuses by some workers.
According to current legislation, a person is not subject to pay any premium on reaching age 70 or when he or she is entitled to a retirement pension or a pension under the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan.
Since 1971, both federal and provincial programs have been substantially improved, among other things the income supplement for persons 65 years or over. The most important improvements include the indexation of old age security pensions and the guaranteed income supplement, the indexation of tax exemptions and the increase in the retirement pension under the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan. For instance, the monthly old age security pension has gone up from $80 in 1971 to about $126 in 1975. The monthly guaranteed income supplement has also risen from $34 for a single person in 1971 to $88 this year. Particularly, the retirement pension paid in accordance with the Canada Pension Plan has increased from $65 in 1971 to $130 a month on July 1, 1975.
Considering all those improvements, the programs would unnecessarily overlap if persons having age 65 were still covered by the unemployment insurance plan. We must also take notice of the fact that it is almost impossible to apply effectively the provisions of the law pertaining to availability and active search for a job to persons of that age since a great many of them are no longer members of the labour force.
In Bill C-69, it is proposed that persons attaining the age of 65 cease to be insured and pay unemployment insurance premiums. Thus persons who will be 65 years of age and will have had at least 20 weeks of insurable employment will receive a special retirement benefit equal to not less than three times the weekly rate of benefit, or an amount of not less than three weekly benefits, if the benefit period has already been established for the claimant.
Mr. Speaker, the old law specified that the age limit would be 70 mainly because at that time that was the age at which people became eligible for old age pension.
I think it would have been more realistic, in all those years, if unemployment insurance had ceased at 69 when people 69 years of age became eligible for pension and so on, gradually lowering each year until 65, which would have made it unnecessary to pass this legislation. However, the main objective was to provide income until retirement. In those days it was believed that the desirable retirement age was 70. And yet, there have been improvements in this area.
It is a fact that whenever the House was dealing with pensions, a number of hon. members, either from the Social Credit Party of Canada or the Progressive Conservative Party, and especially the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), claimed that, in their opinion, the purpose was for workers to become pensioners when they reached age 60. Their main argument was to create jobs when people retired from the labour force at age 60.

October 27, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
What I can hardly understand, although people are invited to retire at age 65, is that these people want to keep on working. Therefore, when they ask to create jobs for people 60 years of age, they are not using the same argument. I wish people who retire at age 60 could have decent lives. If there is a responsibility for people who are 65 years old or over and who are employed, it is not that of an insurance. I see that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is in the House. It is his duty and that of provinces to look after that. We, members of this party, feel that the people who are 65 years of age have worked enough. They deserve a well earned rest after all these many years of working.
Moreover, to allow people of 65 to receive a pension in order to retire more easily, in 1971, those who quit their jobs, at least those who wanted to continue to receive unemployment insurance benefits, were not entitled to do so while being covered by the Canada Pension Plan. That has been corrected since then. Today, at 65, the person who retires is entitled to receive the old age security pension, the full amount of the Canada Pension Plan. Nothing is taken off, except perhaps in one province, and I hope that in that province amendments will be made rapidly to eliminate discrimination against Quebec workers, for instance, whose contributions to the Quebec Pension Plan will be reduced, if they are still working at 65, according to their income, which does not apply in all other provinces of Canada. I wish an amendment in that respect will soon be voted in Quebec.
The age limit for eligibility for unemployment insurance has long been a feature of European plans. In the Federal Republic of Germany, the insured cease to be eligible for benefits when they are 65. Mention is often made of Sweden by our friends of the opposition. There are many plans in that country that are managed by unions, and eligibility for benefits cease at age 65. In Great Britain, for a long time now, the age limit has been tied to the date of eligibility for a pension under the national plan. In Italy, unemployment insurance benefits cease at 60 for men and 55 for women. In all those countries, the age limit is roughly the same as that which is understood in Bill C-69. Unemployment insurance is meant to protect the worker during his active life, and in many European countries, as in Canada, it is felt that other social programs must ensure financial assistance after normal retirement age.
The act as it stands now provides, in the case of persons and dependents, a special rate equal to 75 per cent of the average weekly insurable salary. That rate applies to all those who benefit from unemployment insurance payments during the period of extended payments, and to those who earn the equivalent of or less than a third of the maximum insurable salary during the initial period of benefits.
Since 1971, the government has taken steps to increase the assistance given those who have dependents. The most striking example is family allowances: they have tripled since 1971. For instance, a person with three children aged one to six who used to get $18 a month in 1971 now receives $66.24. In addition, those allowances have been indexed to the cost of living. Those changes, added to higher old age security payments and the guaranteed income supplement meet, far more efficiently, the needs of
people with dependents; they also do away with the reason for a special rate of benefits in their case.
The situation as it exists now in the United States as regards the payment of higher benefits to the recipients with one dependent or more supports the proposal made in Bill C-69. In 41 of the 52 states which have an unemployment insurance plan, benefits are paid at a single rate and the benefits are equivalent to a fixed percentage of the claimant's salary during the qualifying period. In the 11 states which make provision for the dependents, the weekly benefits are nearing or equal to two-thirds of the salary. The rate does not change with the length of demand or the sum of the gains in any state.
The act which was in force before June 27, 1971 provided for an exclusion period of up to six weeks for applicants who left their employment of their own will, lost their job for misbehaviour or refused a suitable job. Normally, this exclusion did not reduce the number of weekly payments the insured person could get; it only delayed the payment of benefits for a period of up to six weeks.
When the new act was enacted in 1971, the maximum period of disqualification was reduced from six to three weeks. The number of weekly benefits payable to claimants was therefore reduced by three. Since 1971, experience has shown that the reduction to three weeks of the disqualification period did not reach its goal, which was to reduce the number of cases where claimants voluntarily left their jobs without reasonable cause, were laid off for cause or refused a suitable job. The number of disqualifications in one year, which is around 300,000, remains dangerously high despite high rates of unemployment and a small proportion of jobs versus number of unemployed.
In view of the proposed amendment to the Canadian program, it is interesting to see how in other countries claimants are disqualified in cases of voluntarily departure without sufficient reason, loss of employment due to misconduct or refusal to accept a suitable job. In the United States, penalties range from simple deferment of benefits for a specified period to complete loss of these benefits.
In other countries, the plan is less harsh, with a reduction in benefits that would otherwise be payable. Certain countries will not pay benefits during the unemployment period or longer, while requiring the claimant to work for a further period in order to requalify. In certain European countries, as Sweden and the Netherlands, the worker who voluntarily leaves his job without sufficient reason does not qualify for benefits. In other countries, the penalty in such cases varies according to the number of occurrences, being more severe on a second or a third voluntary departure.
In a country such as Canada, where unemployment insurance is aimed at favouring manpower mobility, such a formula would not be suitable. The insured persons must of course pay the consequences of loss of revenues through voluntary departure or job refusal. But after some time, they must be able to qualify again under the plan. Another recommendation involves the new threshold for the computation of the government's part of the cost of initial benefits. The principles embodied in the 1971 act, concerning the sharing of the cost between the government and the private sector, are that the private sector must pay for - the share of the basic cost of the plan that relates more

October 27, 1975

directly to the insurance part, and the government for that share of the cost that is more in the nature of a transfer payment. In fact, the federal government assumes the whole cost of those extended benefits paid to training allowance recipients and fishermen.
The private sector takes charge of the whole cost of sickness and maternity benefits, special severance benefits and administrative expenses. The private sector also pays the cost of common initial benefits as long as the unemployment rate is not in excess of 4 per cent. The public sector only pays for those benefits when the unemployment rate is in excess of 4 per cent. The 4 per cent threshold was inferred from comparable costs of the former and new plans for the 1960 to 1969 period. The government think the basic approach of 1971 as well as the concept of the 4 per cent threshold still are valid. However, the 4 per cent threshold stemmed from the economic situation of the decade preceding the introduction of the new legislation.
Since then of course, deep economic and social changes have greatly affected the labour market in general and the unemployment insurance plan in particular. Unemployment rates as well as the cost of unemployment insurance have consequently had a relative tendency to rise. Therefore, if the necessary association between the government and the private sector is to be maintained, in practice as well as in theory, a new sharing concept has to be developed that will be more in keeping with the changing patterns of the social and economic situation.
In view of those remarks, a new unemployment threshold is being proposed to achieve a better balance of initial benefit costs between the government and the private sector. The new rate will be based on the average of monthly rates for each eight years' unemployment period ending on the 30th of June of the year preceding the year for which the threshold is being determined. This moving average will reflect conditions much more closely than the present formula. At the same time it will offer some protection against any abrupt change from year to year. The regular adjustment of the threshold will only affect the division of the cost of initial ordinary payable benefits. The extension benefits to those who are unemployed for a longer period of time will remain entirely payable by the federal government.
Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) referred to this new cost of taxation. He accused the government of transferring $800 million to workers. First, there is no such amount as $800 million. I think the government is still going to save $600 million. That is accurate because in that $600 million they will be able to save about $170 million under all the recommendations included in the amendments to Bill C-69, and the part that employee and employer are going to have to pay is not $800 million but actually $490 million. In that $490 million the workers will not be the only ones paying but they will pay about $210 million. That would be more accurate than $800 million. Employers or corporations or all those employing them will pay 1.4 of that, which means about $280 million that they would have to pay for a figure of $490 million and not $800 million being thrown in, as mentioned earlier.
Unemployment Insurance Act
The financing of unemployment insurance plans in other countries-
I see an hon. member interrupting. He will have his chance to talk afterwards, and I will not interrupt when he is talking.
-especially in the United States of America, is of some interest because of the high rate of unemployment in that country. Many states are having difficulty financing their plans. Every state has a fund. That is where they take their benefits. The reserve of this fund generally increases during periods when unemployment is low and diminishes when it is high. Already 14 states had to borrow money from the federal government to meet their obligations to the unemployed, their reserve being used up. In 16 other states it is estimated that revenues might not be sufficient to pays benefits by the end of December 1976. Those facts show the important effects of high unemployment rates on unemployment insurance funds.
We see how much the protection given through unemployment insurance has changed in the Unites States if we compare the $4.2 billion paid to claimants in 1970 and the $20 billion that are going to be paid in 1975. In the United States, the programs also lay upon the federal government the obligation to pay a part of the benefit costs during high unemployment periods and to help people unemployed during an extended period.
Then, Madam Speaker, the principles underlying unemployment insurance are very similar in every country. However, their implementation should be adapted and modified in view of the changing situation in each country to offer constantly improved protection to the public. The Canadian system compares favourably not only to systems in other countries but also as we can see in Bill C-69, it is adapted to meet existing needs.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to see the minister in the House at this late hour, and delighted to see the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo), as I wish to refer to what these two hon. members said in the second reading debate on this bill. The minister used such jargon as "income support," "income maintenance," and "term insurance" to describe the Unemployment Insurance Act. But he did not increase our understanding of the act or reconcile the paradoxes underlying the Unemployment Insurance Act.
About the only positive thing the minister said in his introduction on second reading was that there will need to be further changes to the unemployment insurance program. Indeed I assure you that there will need to be further changes before we can be excited about some of the things the minister proposed.
I am delighted to see my colleague from Skeena, and was interested to hear her assessment of the minister's speech. I have a good deal in common with the hon. lady. She represents a constituency similar to mine.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: And she is good looking.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
It was interesting to listen to the way she dealt with some of the obvious discrepancies in the act, discrepancies which apply to the areas we represent. It

October 27, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
will be interesting to note what she tells the loggers of Skeena and the service industry of the area. It will be interesting to note the enthusiasm with which the industries of the area learn that not only must they compete for people on the labour market, but that they must compete with the unemployment insurance fund, as people will receive unemployment insurance after the LIP and LEAP programs run out, as will people who have come out of jail.
Industry is facing an awful time trying to find people to work. At the same time the unemployment rate in some localities is between 20 per cent and 22 per cent. I agree with my colleague. She ought to make every effort today and next week to obtain as much LIP money as possible before the program runs out. I agree that the people of the area suffer from problems, but I suggest that those problems have little to do with unemployment. They are of a social nature, and unemployment insurance really should
not be involved.
The bill before the House indicates to us that, as with the case of inflation, the government is adjusting its sails to the prevailing winds of political expediency in dealing with unemployment. It indicates that the government has identified the monster for what it is, and is now asking the House, by introducing Bill C-69, to arm itself with a slingshot with which to attack the beast. The bill, as my colleagues, particularly the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), indicated, will do little to bring the flood under control. And, of all horror stories, that of the government's financial bungling of the UIC fund truly takes the cake.
In 1970 the total outlay in this field was $695 million. The government's contribution was $224 million. In 1975 we expect to be presented with a voucher amounting to $1,150,000,000 in public money. That is the amount needed to sustain the UIC fund if unemployment rises in excess of 4 per cent. Employers and employees are expected to come up with another $2 billion in the current year.
The government with the introduction of Bill C-69 has now, in addition to removing any checks and ceilings from the funds, also abandoned the commitment to strive for a maximum rate of unemployment of 4 per cent in Canada.
Administrative costs as well have kept pace with the orgy of spending. The former minister's white paper of 1970 projected costs of administration of the fund which, over a three-year period, were exceeded by over 100 per cent. Administration costs for 1974 estimated at $74 million actually cost $162 million. I will not bore the House with long lists of the shameful performance of the government.
The hon. member for Skeena made reference to daily dealings with the unemployment office by talking of bureaucrats who try to administer. It was interesting to note how excited she became about travel expenses being paid to people to get their appeal referred to the umpire. In her part of the country and mine, people cannot get to the appeal board. Some must travel 700 miles-and then there is always a unanimous decision by the appeal board.
We have told the minister that people cannot get their appeals heard. For those in the northern parts of Canada, there is no such thing as an appeal to the Unemployment Insurance Commission or the appeal board. How, not
having been able to get to the appeal board, having been turned down before the appeal gets started, will they go to the umpire, particularly when the decision is always unanimous, as it is in Prince George? The chairman will not consider having the appeal referred to some other tribunal.
With regard to the orgy in spending, for those of us who daily deal with the UIC office, this does not come as a surprise. Armies of dedicated managers, adjudicators, counsellors, commissioners, agents, clerks, and janitors man the regional, district and local offices, carrying out the intent of an act, the intention of which has never been defined. Are they employees of an insurance corporation, or is it a social service they are providing? Is it a Manpower management agency or a relief agency for those who can either not find work or have no intention of working as long as benefits flow freely from the UIC commission?
A major division of the UIC army deals with abuses of the act. All of us know that abuses of the act present the major outlay, not only in the administration but also in benefits paid.
I wish to examine some of the obvious abuses. I will put them in two categories. The first deals with abuses permissible under the act. Unless the government addresses itself to this question, the flood will continue to flow over the dam. I have concerned myself with this question for some time.
In 1973 I canvassed my constituents with a questionnaire that asked some very serious questions. For example, I asked "How do you look at the unemployment insurance program (1) as similar to a savings program where you should eventually get something back?" Thirty-four per cent replied "yes". They felt that if you pay into the scheme, you should get something back. The other part of the question was "(2) as a life insurance policy where nothing is paid unless you are out of work involuntarily." The greater percentage, 72 per cent, was honest and said it should indeed be the intention of the act.
I also asked, "Do you consider the services of Canada Manpower adequate in matching job seekers with jobs?" Sixty-one per cent said no because it simply does not work. The services in my part of the country are not synchronized, nor are they anywhere else. I also asked, "Do you feel the services of Canada Manpower and of the Unemployment Insurance Commission should be combined?" to which 71 per cent replied yes.
Some people in Canada use the service as a bank, storing up leisure time. Let me give some examples of what I mean. The first is a family I know who live in the city of Victoria, British Columbia. This is no reflection on my colleague from British Columbia because the story is not very pretty. The man has reached middle age and is in a better than middle income category, earning between $35,000 and $40,000 a year. The children have left home and the wife is bored. The husband travels a lot and she is home alone.
To overcome her boredom she works in the local butcher shop for about eight months of the year. When her husband is home, she likes to be with him. She has an agreement with her employer whereby she quits her job and for four months of the year collects unemployment
October 27, 1975

insurance. She does not necessarily want the unemployment insurance or to make an abuse of the fund, but she is trapped in the system. What alternative does she have?
Another example involves some friends we were visiting in Prince George in the constituency of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mrs. Campagnolo). The woman told me to observe what was going on across the street. A middle aged couple were loading a car and a very expensive silver trailer. They were about to embark on a journey to an undisclosed destination. It was not that cold, but the woman had on a fancy mink coat, apparently wanting to protect herself between the house and the car. The husband, a fisherman, earned about $40,000 a year. He is a good fisherman and deserves that income. The wife works in a supermarket. At the time they left Prince George, they were both receiving unemployment insurance. This is one of the permissible abuses.
I have just one more example. It involves construction workers in Powell River. Because of climatic conditions, they have cyclical employment, working seven, eight or nine months of the year. Because of the make-up of their jobs, the income they earn is much higher than that of someone who works all year. In addition to earning between $25,000 and $30,000 a year, they collect unemployment for four months. That is another example of permissible abuses. May I call it ten o'clock, Madam Speaker.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-BILINGUAL AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL COMMUNICATIONS-SUGGESTED RESUMPTION OF STUDY BY COMMITTEE
AIR TRANSPORT-BILINGUAL AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL COMMUNICATIONS-SUGGESTED RESUMPTION OF STUDY BY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the outset of this short debate I should like to state that I question the use of the French language as a means of air traffic control. While sympathetic to the cultural aims of Canada's linguistic minority I believe that the highly technical field of aviation, with its critical safety factor, is no proper arena for the introduction of bilingualism in the pursuit of social ends.
Until I, and a good many people like myself, can be convinced otherwise, I cannot accept or condone the concept of bilingual air to ground communication. Introduction of such a concept would compromise aviation safety and in aviation the aim is, surely, to remove any compromise with safety. I believe there is a real danger involved in the continued and wider use of two languages in air-ground communications. One should not be so much concerned with personal or collective language rights to be found in the Official Languages Act as with personal or collective responsibility toward safety.
Adjournment Debate
The demand in one specialized sector that the use of French be authorized for regional aviation operations is dangerous. Superficially, it might appear harmless for the Ministry of Transport to allow the use of French, say, between Baie Comeau control tower and a member of the local airplane club, but it is neither desirable nor possible to work out a system catering to local pride in language without coming into hazardous conflict with general practice.
For whatever motives the newly organized group of air traffic controllers in Quebec wants French to be given equal recognition with English, it is willing to close its eyes to world-wide procedures designed to make aviation safer by eliminating language conflicts in communications. If choosing English discriminates against the French of French Canada it is also unfair to the Germans, Dutch, Spanish, Italians, Portuguese and members of all other language groups who must communicate with pilots or control towers during split second take-offs and landings in international flights. It appears that the Quebec controllers are aiming for a change in the Official Languages Act to expand the use of French.
All this may sound rather bigoted against the use of French but I assure you, Madam Speaker, that it is not. The main thing we must all keep first and foremost in our minds is the importance of aviation safety. I happen to feel that to compromise aviation safety by using a language other than English is at some point in time likely to be detrimental or fatal to the Canadian flying public. I believe that to make an exception for Quebec will merely isolate private pilots in that province who are described as the main beneficiaries of the proposals, making it more difficult for them ever to fly outside the province of Quebec. Regardless of a natural pride in one's mother tongue, English is the language of communication in aviation, as it is at sea.
What concerns many people is the question of what would happen if the use of the French language were to be expanded to more than the five airports presently employing it. What about the major airports in the Province of Quebec? For that matter, what about the rest of Canada?
It is interesting to note-and the government may attach some importance to it-that the Flying Farmers of Canada, a large organization composed of farm people using light aircraft in all the provinces across Canada, has come out full square in favour of the use of the English language in air-ground communications. The association has passed a resolution stating that it would prefer all air traffic controllers to be instructed in English only. The association makes it clear that the flying farmers are not speaking out against French but against the use of any language other than English-the universal language of aviation.
I would urge the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Goodale), who is in his place, to come clean in the debate tonight and to state the government's intentions. The committee (BILCOM) has failed and it appears it is divided not on the safety factor but on the language factor. We see a minority report coming out of Project BILCOM advocating the use of the French language much more extensively than at the present time. The writer of that report talks more about the Official Languages Act than he does about air safety.

October 27, 1975
Adjournment Debate
I cannot and will not condone what is taking place at the present time in the province of Quebec in terms of air safety. I believe that if the experiment is allowed to continue lives may be lost, and an even greater fear is that at some point in time the Ministry of Transport may be talked into allowing the use of the French language to expand throughout the province of Quebec to the major international airports.
For these reasons I would urge the government to reverse its stand on the aspect of bilingual air-ground communications before someone is seriously hurt.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-BILINGUAL AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL COMMUNICATIONS-SUGGESTED RESUMPTION OF STUDY BY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me say as I begin to reply to the hon. member this evening that I very much agree with his general concern for safety, and I assure him that the minister and the Ministry of Transport do so as well. However, I cannot agree with the hon. member's interpretation of the facts in the particular case to which he has referred.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) intends to continue investigation into the safety aspect of the use of two languages during air-ground communications, and consultation with the aviation community in that regard. The decision to introduce further changes to the existing language situation will not be made before the most exhaustive examination indicates clearly that such changes will appear to be safe and will in fact be safe.
The minister has said in reply to the hon. member's earlier question that while, where convenient and possible, the ministry would want to make French language facilities available to pilots, the uppermost consideration must be conditions of safety in flight. The minister further indicated that discussions would be continued with all interested groups involved in the air industry to demonstrate that this is what we are trying to accomplish.
Prior to its dissolution, the safety committee to which the hon. member has referred agreed on the provision of bilingual advisory service by air radio stations in the province of Quebec. The ministry has prepared a plan to implement this service but intends to brief the aviation associations prior to implementation.
Any extension of bilingual VFR control beyond the present five airport areas in the province of Quebec will be the subject of separate consultation with aviation associations, and will be contemplated only where fully consistent with safety.
The areas of Dorval and Mirabel airports will continue to be excluded from any such consideration of expansion. The more complex problem of the introduction of the French language into air-ground communications during flight operations under instrument flight rules will require extensive study and use of the air traffic service simulator and the joint participation of the aviation community before it can be determined that this change is feasible.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BILL RELATING TO HONG KONG AND EUROPEAN PRISONERS OF WAR
VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BILL RELATING TO HONG KONG AND EUROPEAN PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, July 29, as recorded in Hansard at

page 8023, I put this question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald):
Will the minister consider tabling, before the House rises for its recess, the government's bill implementing the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs with respect to Canadian prisoners of war, both Hong Kong and European?
The minister's reply was to the effect that the recess was just about upon us and he doubted if it would be possible to meet my request before we rose for the summer. However, he did say this in respect of the legislation about which I questioned him:
It is being prepared, for presentation to cabinet.
Sometime later, on Wednesday, October 15, I put another question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs in which I reminded him of the exchange on July 29 to which I have just referred. I concluded by asking him my question in these words:
Can he say whether a bill implementing these recommendations will be introduced shortly?
The minister replied, as it appears on page 8229, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the report referred to by the hon. member is presently under consideration by the government.
Perhaps I might take a moment or two to indicate what that report was all about. All of us are familiar with it but it might be well to have its terms on the record briefly at this point. It is a report which was approved unanimously by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. It was submitted to the House on Thursday, June 12. The report followed an extensive study of the Hermann report on the whole question of what we should be doing for Canadians who were prisoners of war in Europe, and also whether we should be improving the pensions of Canadians who were prisoners of war in Hong Kong.
We made four recommendations. The first was that there should be a new act of parliament to deal specifically with the case of former prisoners of war. Second, we proposed that the compensation arrangements to veterans who were prisoners of the Japanese should be improved. At the present time there is a 50 per cent pension guaranteed to anyone who was a prisoner of the Japanese, but anyone who already has an assessed disability pension does not receive it on top of that 50 per cent. Our recommendation is that the 50 per cent would be given everyone who was at Hong Kong and that any assessed disability pension should be on top of that 50 per cent, with a ceiling of 100 per cent on the total pension.
Our third recommendation is that there should be established scales of pensions for those who were prisoners of war in Europe. We arrived at a formula which suggested that in respect of incarceration up to one and one-half years it should be 10 per cent, in respect of incarceration for a period from one and one-half years to two and one-half years it should be 15 per cent, and in the case of incarceration for a period of two and one-half years or over it should be 20 per cent. An assessed disability pension would be on top of these percentages.
Our fourth recommendation was that a basic change should be made in the provision of pensions for widows of veterans. The general rule now is that unless a veteran's
October 27, 1975

disability pension is 50 per cent or more-and for a technical reason that is the same as 48 per cent-there is no survivor's pension as a right for the widow. We are recommending this be changed and that there be in effect a pro rata pension for the widow of any veteran on a disability pension.
I am not arguing the case for these four points tonight. I do not think this is necessary. I simply felt they should be part of what is on the record at this point. We think we did a good job in the committee. We heard many witnesses. We sorted all the evidence and tried to arrive at a compromise where there were differences.
One thing which pleases me is that the member of the committee who happened to move the motion which received the unanimous support of the committee, who then was a private member, is now a member of the cabinet. I refer to the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), now Minister of National Revenue. I welcome the smile on the face of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) because in him he knows he has a supporter for this cause.
My plea to the minister tonight is a straightforward one. I do not stand here arguing with him. I believe he is just as anxious for this legislation as I am, but it is a matter of deep concern that so many months can go by before action is taken in respect of a matter of this kind. The Hermann report was dated 1973 although we did not receive it until 1974. The recommendation of the standing committee was made on June 12, 1975, and here we are almost at the end of October. These veterans, especially the Hong King veterans, literally die off because of their experience as prisoners of war. There were many who were prisoners of war in Europe who were encouraged by the report of our committee, but what they need is for the legislation to come into effect.
I am happy that the minister has been able to say to me on two occasions that the matter is before cabinet. I hope he knows that he has the support of the entire House, and if he cannot tell us tonight on what day cabinet will let him bring in the legislation, I hope he will be ready to give that answer the next time I put the question to him, because he knows that if he does not bring it in soon there certainly will be a next time for this same question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BILL RELATING TO HONG KONG AND EUROPEAN PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to reply to the question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) requesting a bill relating to Canadian prisoners or war in Europe and Hong Kong.
Hon. members will recall that the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs at its meeting on June 22, 1972, requested that a study be undertaken to identify any physiological or psychological long term effects which their incarceration may have had on ex-prisoners of war of the European theatre, numbering approximately 7,500. The government accepted this recommendation and on January 31, 1973, the study was undertaken by Dr. J. Douglas Hermann, a distinguished Canadian surgeon. Dr. Hermann's report was received by the government and tabled in the House of Commons on Monday, November 18, 1974. It was subsequently referred to the standing committee
Adjournment Debate
for study on Wednesday, March 26, 1975, and the committee reported back to the House on Thursday, June 12, 1975.
In the meantime I have held consultations on this very important subject with my colleagues. At the present time this, along with other government proposals, must be examined carefully in the light of the recently announced guidelines. I would hope, as would other members of the House, that the request for compensation for ex-prisoners of war will not become a victim of our financial restrictions.
I hope to have something more definite to announce before too long.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-TREATMENT OF EMPLOYEES TAKING FRENCH LANGUAGE TRAINING-GOVERNMENT ACTION
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-TREATMENT OF EMPLOYEES TAKING FRENCH LANGUAGE TRAINING-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on October 16 I directed a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) with regard to the application of the Official Languages Act vis-a-vis CNR employees of the passenger sales department at Winnipeg and the unjust treatment they were receiving under the Official Languages Act, and also respecting the 1973 resolution which was to protect unilingual civil servants but which is offering no protection to them at all.
I have received a letter from the minister in which he says that as a result of changes in the transcontinental train schedule the hours of service to the public of the Winnipeg ticket and reservation offices were reduced. This resulted in a decrease in two counter and three telephone positions. The necessary advance notice was provided to the brotherhood in accordance with the existing arrangement on operation changes.
There is confusion here because the brotherhood has contacted the members of the CNR department in Winnipeg and they have told him they are not covered by the 1973 resolution which was passed in parliament. The spokesmen for the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Workers state that CNR is in the throes of establishing six bilingual positions in Winnipeg, but so far they have designated only three.
The minister went on to say that as regards language rating only two ticket office personnel have completed the presently available French courses and they are considered bilingual for the positions they occupy. No employees who have taken any of the language training have been notified that they are bilingual, and if they had been designated bilingual it would not be necessary for CNR to hire bilingual persons off the street to take positions in this department, with job security, and to get all the overtime in the department. That is why this ridiculous document was passed in June of 1973, a document not worth the paper it is written on. It was never intended to protect unilingual civil servants at all. If the government had any intention of protecting them, it would have made this document part of the Official Languages Act, and made it law.
I would like to point out that I voted against the Official Languages Act. This is one of the reasons why we pointed out at the time that the federal government had no inten-

Adjournment Debate
tion of protecting unilingual civil servants, and that is why I did not support it at that time, and I have been proven right to date.
The letter from the minister goes on to say that CN has had more than 10 years of a very strong language training program. If the CNR had a very strong language training program, it would be providing these employees with the 12 month training which is called for in the 1973 resolution, but it is not doing this.
The minister goes on to say that they will allow language training which allows for training as long as it is deemed necessary for the position in question and remains within the spirit and intent of the resolution referred to by me.
However, the CNR is not providing this 12 month training. It is hiring people off the street to take these bilingual positions. I would suggest to the parliamentary secretary that he give the message to the Minister of Transport that it would certainly improve employee relations, and departmental efficiency and morale, if CNR officials met with these employees. This has not been done. There has been no contact with them at all, and I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that the CNR officials have not provided the minister with the proper information. I would say that he has been sold a bill of goods. This letter I have been provided with is contradictory and does not cover any of the points I have raised.
One French person has just quit the CNR, and the CNR will not offer this position to any of the men in that department. This letter says that two of them are declared bilingual. Why will they not give them this position if two of the employees have been declared bilingual?
Further, five workers whose jobs were abolished last month were not given the opportunity to exercise their seniority over bilingual workers in the same department, and I should also like to point out that every one of these employees is willing to take this French language training. They want to take the 12 month training program so that they can hang on to their jobs.
There is absolutely no requirement for the French language to be used at all in the Winnipeg office. I am told by these employees that they would be better off if they were learning German, so whatever training they get is just an absolute waste of money, and the whole operation is just another farce and a sham.
These employees have had to find jobs elsewhere within the railroad. One girl had to take a job driving a truck because she was not allowed to stay in her department, and she wants to take this 12 month training course.
In 1973 the passenger service centre hired three French speaking workers. Railway officials assured other workers that the hirings would not affect their job security, but it is doing so. Up to two months ago they were telling us that everything would be all right. However, more lay-offs or job transfers are feared in the near future.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will ask the minister to get back to Mr. Bandeen, the president of CNR, just to find out what is going on in this particular department.
There were assurances from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) back in 1968. He stated that unilingual civil servants would be protected. He said that despite the extension of the bilingual system in the public service, protection would be given to unilingual civil servants. He said that achievement of federal bilingual plans must not involve any prejudice to the careers of civil servants who are not bilingual and who have devoted many years to the public service. This is not in effect in this passenger service department of the CNR in Winnipeg. I will point it out again, and I hope the parliamentary secretary will recommend to the Minister of Transport, that he should raise the issue in cabinet. If he is sincere in protecting unilingual civil servants he will have this resolution made law and become a part of the Official Languages Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-TREATMENT OF EMPLOYEES TAKING FRENCH LANGUAGE TRAINING-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very interested in many of the comments of the hon. member but I regret that I must disagree pretty strongly with the tenor in which he delivered them. I do not think they convey an accurate assessment of the situation regarding CNR employees in Winnipeg, which I think requires some clarification.
As the hon. member mentioned, the minister has written to him in considerable detail on the points he raised in the House on other occasions. It must be made clear that there have in fact been no lay-offs in this particular department. As a result of changes in the transcontinental train schedule, the hours of service to the public of the Winnipeg ticket and reservation offices were reduced. This resulted in a decrease in two counter and three telephone positions. The necessary advance notice was provided the brotherhood in accordance with the existing arrangements on operational change. The incumbents involved in the staff reductions have since secured employment in other departments.
With reference to points raised by the hon. member on language training, the two ticket office personnel have completed the present available French courses. They are considered bilingual for the positions they occupy.
I was interested in the hon. member's assertion that these particular employees had not been officially advised of their status. I will certainly take notice of that and pursue it to see what is involved. The CN has had language training programs for over ten years. These programs allow for training for as long as is deemed necessary for the position in question, and remain within the spirit and intent of the resolution passed by parliament in June, 1973.
Finally, Madam Speaker, I think it would be useful to point out that CN has in fact established three positions above and beyond the union agreement which require fluent French. Only one of these positions is presently vacant and the employees in question in the sales department did not apply for it.
